utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, am I going to be allowed a little more time, as I requested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can have another hour and three quarters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I have a large number of documents here, so I'll have to make a selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Williams, you said that the situation on the Sarajevo front became much worse in the second half of 1994, and I think you said in that regard -- and you say this in your statement on page 7, paragraph 6, in fact. I'd like to draw your attention to that for it to be easier for you to follow my question. As I said, you say that it worsened visibly, because as you said, the Bosnian Serbs closed the only ground route across Mount Igman, allowing passage only to military transports belonging to the UN. I think that's what you said, words to that effect, Mr. Williams. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, my question is this: Why in your statement did you omit to explain why this road across Mount Igman was closed in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was closed for a variety of reasons, but the principal reason that I recall was that it -- the road had become increasingly difficult and dangerous to traverse. I would draw your attention, for example, to an incident on July the 27th, when a convoy came under sustained gunfire from Bosnian Serb positions and a British soldier tragically lost his life in that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just going to read out something and ask you whether you know about this. It's something that this man wrote, Mr. David Fraser, in fact, in his statement says the following: That in the morning on the 6th of October, 1994 a team of the BH army launched an attack on the camp of Bosnian Serbs on Mount Igman and they left 17 dead behind them. The Muslims passed through the demilitarised zone in order to reach that area. They passed the terrain which the Serbs handed over at a time when an agreement had been reached in February 1994. Now, is that a truthful explanation of what happened or not? And you have this in David Fraser's statement.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: David Fraser's statement is not familiar with -- to me, but I would confirm the incident that you referred to in -- on the 6th of October. In fact, I recall well being in Sarajevo that day with Mr. Akashi, and he went to see President Izetbegovic to protest strongly about the incident which you refer to. I mean, I think you're correct in saying that there was fighting along this road involving the two warring sides, but I have to say to you that fire and harassment of UN convoys came only from one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this is correct and not correct at the same time. But let's not waste time on that. There are records about that and facts too. Now, as you did have this piece of information from the explanation you've just given - I gather you did have information to that effect - did you intentionally fail to explain the entirety of the event, or was that quite simply a bias form of presenting it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just consider this question. What is the bias you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it says that the Serbs cut off the sole road across the ground and that they just let the UN through, whereas no explanation is given why this land route was closed off and in fact that it was closed off precisely because of the event that Mr. Fraser describes, that is to say, a UN officer writing in his own statement about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the question is to the witness: Dr. Williams, you didn't mention this in your statement. Was there any particular reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no particular reason for it at all, and I would repeat that I think the closure of the road arose from several circumstances. Mr. Milosevic is correct to draw attention to this very serious incident on the 6th of October, but I would repeat, the prime reason for the closure of the road was repeated attacks on UN humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't quite understand that, because the Serbs closed -- if the Serbs closed off the road, now, why would they close off the road and as you yourself say they let the UN convoys pass through. They were the only ones that were allowed through. They didn't allow anybody else through; that is to say, the Muslim transports at all. And you said that yourself, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything you think you can add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot add anything further to that point, Judge May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you made your point. The witness has agreed with what you said, that there was this incident. Now, spending further time on it doesn't really assist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you happen to know, Mr. Williams, that the Muslims did not withdraw from that part of the demilitarised zone, not even after protests and meetings that were held with Delic and Divljak and General Michael Rose and the French general, Gobillard, on the 8th of October, 1994. So they held negotiations, these two negotiating sides, the two generals and the others, and not even then did they withdraw. Do you know about that? Just give me a yes or no answer and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I hope it's not being challenged that the Muslim forces used the peace agreement of 1994 in order to take up positions in the demilitarised zone itself.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which according to agreement was under Serb control and in order to sign the agreement they had passed it over to UN control. So the Serbs handed over the control of this demilitarised zone to the -- to UNPROFOR, and the Muslims used this, took advantage of that, to take control of it and to make something -- score a point for themselves, give themselves the military advantage. Do you know about that? Just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you that there were many probing actions and infiltrations of the demilitarised zone by Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Tell me, why are you distorting events and showing them as aggressive acts on one side, on the part of one side, namely the Bosnian Serbs, when your employees and staff deny this in argumentative fashion, according to what I've just read out, and you yourself say that it is indeed correct and true?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think because you cannot separate the incidents which you have been describing and the pattern of behaviour that you've alluded to from the fact that this was a city under siege and there is no doubt what were the forces that were besieging the city. You also fail to mention that throughout this period, from October 1994 onwards, the UN was having increasing difficulties in operating the air bridge into Sarajevo airport, and that -- those difficulties arose because of obstacles placed by the Bosnian Serbs and frequent threats to UN aircraft from Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did they shoot down a plane at all, Mr. Williams? Did the Serbs shoot down a plane during the war at all belonging to the UN or anybody else, any other kind of organisation, international one or whatever? Did they shoot down a plane?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you of several instances. I can tell you not of planes being shot down, thankfully. But on the 17th of April, 1994, for example, the force commander's plane coming into Sarajevo was directly shot at by Bosnian Serb forces. That was raised immediately with Dr. Karadzic, he did not deny the incident. On the 12th of March, 1995, an aircraft carrying Mr. Akashi into Sarajevo was directly shot at from Bosnian Serb positions, causing one of his bodyguards to be seriously injured. And my recollection is that that officer had to be medevaced to the United States, in fact, such were the nature of his injuries. More often than not the threat was made very, very clear by General Mladic. We had withdrawn our guarantees for safety for UN aircraft. And then Mr. Akashi and the force commander had to make the judgement that it was too dangerous to fly into Sarajevo. I would also point you to the fact that in the latter part of 1994 onwards, especially from October, Serb air defences around Sarajevo were reinforced and adopted a more threatening position to UN aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, what I asked you was whether they shot down any planes, and you're now explaining all the things that took place and all the incidents. Incidents are possible in war. But as far as I know, not a single plane was shot down, according to my information. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would confirm that not a single plane was shot down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these Serbs that you call the aggressors and so forth, they were also citizens of Sarajevo and citizens of the surrounding areas who lived there in those areas and in Sarajevo on their own territory, at home. So they weren't -- they weren't, in fact, waging siege against their own city. It was the frontline that was located there, regardless of the fact that of course any shelling was to be denounced. And we did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's come to a question. The point which is apparently being made is that it wasn't a siege. I don't quite understand it, but maybe you could throw some light on it, Dr. Williams, I don't know. It wasn't a siege; it was local people, I suppose it's being said, defending their own homes, and therefore it couldn't have been a siege. I'm not sure it's a question you can answer. But if you can make any useful comment, please do. If not, just say you can't possibly answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic is absolutely correct in saying that many, many Serbs lived on the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation line. It's also worth pointing out that there were Serbs who lived in Bosnian government controlled parts of the city, and indeed that there was a Bosnian Serb civic council within Sarajevo that frequently made comments and statements, one of which is, I believe, in Exhibit 21 of my -- attached to my statements yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And just let me add, or, rather, ask you, Mr. Williams, were the Serbs able to leave Sarajevo of their own free will, the ones living in Sarajevo, the part of Sarajevo that was under the control of Muslim forces; could they? Were they able to leave if they felt like it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's rather -- rather an odd question because it was -- it was very, very difficult for anyone to leave the city of Sarajevo throughout most of the three years from 1992 to the autumn of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether they had the freedom to leave Sarajevo. Were they at liberty to leave Sarajevo, in view of the positions held by the authorities and the Muslim authorities, in fact? Were they free to leave? It's another matter whether it was difficult to leave and whether they could or couldn't, but were they free to leave if they so desired?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that like most citizens of the city of Sarajevo throughout this period, it was nigh on impossible for them to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because the authorities wouldn't permit them to, the Muslim authorities of Sarajevo; isn't that right, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that there were restrictions on all citizens in the city of Sarajevo. There were the difficulties that there was virtually no access to and from the city for citizens. I do not recall specific restrictions being imposed upon Serb inhabitants in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do know, I'm sure, that the Serb military commanders and Serb civilian authorities kept repeating the fact that citizens who wished to leave should be allowed to do so and that they guaranteed them free passage and safety and security; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were some statements to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know that General Michael Rose on the 5th of February, 1994 - that is to say, when you were occupying your post, the one you have explained to us - proposed a peace plan for Sarajevo, and as far as my information tells me and as far as I've noted down here, it was composed of four basic elements: A cease-fire; that was under number two, the second point -- that was to come into force on the 10th of February. B was within a radius of 20 kilometres; that is to say, that should be the zone from which all heavy weapons would be withdrawn and placed under UN control. Under C, point C, was that the UN troops should be deployed at key points between the two warring sides; and D, to set up a joint commission composed of the representatives of Serbs, Muslims, and led by the command of the Bosnian sector in order to discuss the details of a peace plan and compile them. Do you know that within the frameworks of that plan collection centres were established for the collection of heavy weaponry and equipment? Are you aware of all that? Do you know about all that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true and correct what Mr. Thomas Roy says in his statement on several occasions, in several parts, because you took constant shelling of Sarajevo in 1994 and 1995, that the peace plan dated back to February 1994, and he emphasises that, that it wielded significant influence on Sarajevo and that the Bosnian Serbs ceased to shell the town and did not continue at the same level and to the same degree as was previously the case. Do you know about that? Did information of that kind reach you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a clue who Thomas Roy is. With regard to the information you ascribe to him, I -- I think you're wrong in summarising my view that there was constant shelling in 1994/1995. In fact, I hope I was careful to say that there was a substantial reduction in shelling following the February 1994 Sarajevo crisis, precisely because a lot of the heavy weaponry was drawn back from the surroundings of the city. This didn't mean to say that it didn't happen from time to time, but it was greatly reduced from February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you in fact agree with the observation. Now, I'm not clear in the differences in your statement between what you say in your statement and what you're now saying. I don't quite understand. Now, Mr. Williams, on page 4 of your statement, you refer to the April talks held in Belgrade which related to the Gorazde enclave. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember that those negotiations which you point to were -- that there were meetings before that in April on the Sarajevo -- at Sarajevo airport between the generals, Delic on the Muslim side, in fact, General Mladic, and General Rose, that those were the preliminary meetings with a view to resolving the Gorazde situation? So General Michael Rose at Sarajevo airport initiated agreements with both commanders, Delic and Mladic, the three of them, in fact, from the 7th to the 9th of April were at Sarajevo airport meeting and holding meetings in order to solve the Gorazde problem.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct. And of course there were also meetings between Mr. Akashi and Dr. Karadzic around this period in Pale. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know why these talks and negotiations did not end in a solution of any kind, that they didn't bear fruit and a solution wasn't found? Why not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My very clear recollection is that the primary reason why these talks failed was that Bosnian Serb forces continually pressed their attack on the safe area of Gorazde. I think the reports are very, very clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that a solution was not found for the simple reason that the representatives of Republika Srpska or, rather, General Mladic insisted on a cease-fire not only for Gorazde but also for the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the Muslim side did not want to have a general cease-fire and truce? Wasn't that how it was or not? Is what I'm saying correct or not, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct in summarising the position of General Mladic and the Bosnian Serbs. I have to say I find it an extraordinary tactic that one side in a conflict continues with a most brutal attack on a declared UN safe area deliberately targeting civilians and is unwilling to stop those attacks except on the other side agreeing to a general cease-fire throughout Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your very own senior military observer says that the Muslims did not want a general cease-fire until they reinforced their own combat lines. This is an explanation that is quite different, and it was proffered by a senior military observer; is that correct, Mr. Williams, or not? Do you agree with this position or not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that position at all, and I'm not even sure who you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, Mr. Williams, that in connection with an article published in the Washington Post by John Parfot [phoen] from the foreign policy service of Washington Post, didn't you investigate that? Because it criticised the role of the USA and NATO in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in the vicinity of Sarajevo. Please just give me a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to follow your question for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll have to clarify the question, Mr. Milosevic. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking whether it's correct that you started an investigation in relation to an article published by the Washington Post which had criticised the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When, Mr. Milosevic? When was this article published, so we can try and identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it's the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it's John Pomfritt, Saturday, April the 30th of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got it in our papers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's in a vast amount of Rule 68 material. I don't know whether the Prosecution have it to hand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it right here. This UNPROFOR confidential material addressed to Mr. Yasushi Akashi from Mr. Michael Williams, director for information, and the subject is: Washington Post Article Inquiry. That's the document that I received from Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it correct that within that investigation -- so this is a document of yours. You do remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not fair on the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We are looking for the document. And if Mr. Milosevic would be kind enough to provide us the ERN number, we can do it quicker. And I would ask that any questions regarding the document be postponed until a copy can be put before the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I now do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has got a copy; we haven't. But we'll see how we get on. What's the -- give us the ERN number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] R0101447. That's the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have it here, and I'll have copies made for the Court immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has got the copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to save time. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So with that investigation, did you talk to Mr. -- to General Michael Rose?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at item 16.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 16, yes. Paragraph 16 of your statement, of your report, rather, the report that you submitted to Mr. Akashi. It says: [In English] "General Rose expressed more generally his view on the conflicts and mentioned that he was convinced that prior to events in Gorazde the Serbs were ready for a general cease-fire agreement and that he was confident that both sides would eventually return to the negotiating table. This appears to be consistent with ideas appearing in the article to the effect that Serb forces were ready for peace despite the recent attack on Gorazde." [Interpretation] So is that beyond dispute, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, if you would allow me now, I will comment on the document that you've brought before me. This document relates to an off-the-record briefing that General Rose gave to journalists in Sarajevo. As is often the case in these off-the-record briefings that senior officials give, some of it becomes public and perhaps General Rose on occasion was perhaps more indiscreet than he could have been. Now, to refer to the specific paragraph, paragraph 16, that Mr. Milosevic draws my attention to, as Mr. Milosevic said, General Rose said that prior to events in Gorazde Serbs were ready for a general cease-fire agreement. I think that was his assessment. He was basing that, I believe, on the conclusion of the Sarajevo crisis in February 1994 and also on the fact that in March 1994 a peace agreement had been concluded between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats. His hope was that that would lead similarly, in a short period of time, to a peace agreement between Bosnian government forces and the Serbs. Alas, that didn't take place. What was the fundamental reason why that didn't take place? It was because of the attack on Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's -- we'll have a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please have this exhibited, Mr. May. I'm not asking for the entire report of Mr. Williams to be exhibited, but at least paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Williams. What you said just now, isn't that a confirmation, and also what General Rose says, and you quote in your report not only General Rose but you also state yourself that the initial talks about Gorazde were held at Butmir airport and failed not because of the Serbs but because of the Muslim delegation that did not want to agree to a general cease-fire for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given my assessment of those talks at the airport in Sarajevo and I don't think I have anything further to add on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your opinion, was the reason why the Muslims did not agree to a general cease-fire or even negotiations about a general cease-fire for Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had originally been proposed by the Serbs, was the reason for that that they were expecting NATO strikes against Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- I must say, as you're persisting in this line of questioning, I've spent a lot of my professional life looking at wars and conflicts in various parts of the world. I do find it quite extraordinary that you're trying to put this suggestion that the only way that the Bosnian Serbs would agree to stop attacking - I repeat - a UN safe area and deliberately targeting civilian officials, both of which I regard, by the way, as completely uncontested facts, you say that the only way to avoid this is to agree a complete cease-fire and a settlement throughout Bosnia. I find that an extraordinary supposition and one which, again in my experience of conflict and so on, I couldn't see that working in any part of the world in any conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, that's not what I'm saying at all. You know that the war was waged all over Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serbs had proposed a general cease-fire. Are you holding this against them, this kind of a proposal for a general cease-fire, that is to say, not only in Gorazde but in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? So that would include Gorazde too. Gorazde was not an exception of any kind. I'm not claiming that that's the reason, as you had put it, for the attack on Gorazde, I mean. Or do I know, for that matter. So you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. What is it you want to ask the witness? Would you make it clear. What is it you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, we are going to look at the question of Gorazde, apart from everything else too. And by the way, it was resolved with my assistance. But I'm asking Mr. Williams --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's get to Gorazde, instead of going round and round this point. Yes. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's get to the question of Gorazde. We are going to get to the question of Gorazde. But before that I'm asking Mr. Williams whether he's aware of the fact that fighting took place not only in Gorazde but throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think we need trouble with that. I think that's accepted. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groome produced a document here dated the 17th of April. I think that this was in tab 14. I'm not going to dwell on it. Akashi is writing and sending a copy to Annan and all the rest and he's reporting about a meeting with Karadzic and Izetbegovic. And since Akashi talked to both political leaders, that is to say, both to Karadzic and to Izetbegovic, you commented upon this report and you said that it gave a very gloomy forecast, in terms of the entire situation. That's what I wrote down here on the margins. You said that the situation was very gloomy, very difficult; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, Mr. Williams, that Mr. Akashi actually talked to me, asking me to help resolve that question? Or rather, do you know that Mr. Akashi from time to time - I would even say frequently, in view of the fact that he was in Zagreb - wished to consult me, to hear my views and to ask for certain assistance and intervention that I could possibly exercise vis-a-vis the leadership of Republika Srpska? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, take a look, then, at the report of the Secretary-General of the UN related to Resolution 913 from 1994. It is also provided here. So let's just go through this briefly. So in paragraph 3 he says that, "On the 22nd and 23rd of April, my Special Representative" - "my" meaning the Secretary-General's. It's the Secretary-General who is saying this, so it is the special representative, "Yasushi Akashi, and the commander of UNPROFOR, General Bertrand de Lapresle, met in Belgrade with civilian and military authorities and the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, at the invitation of President Slobodan Milosevic, the president of the Republic of Serbia." And then he moves on to say what was achieved. But before that, I would like to draw your attention to page 10 of this same report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which tab are we in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's tab 20, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 10, paragraph 19. Since the Secretary-General explains in quite a bit of detail what the situation was like, actually, he says, 19, "On May 14, 1994, my Special Representatives spoke with President Milosevic, who had assisted" -- that's what he says: "who had assisted" -- [In English] "On the Belgrade meeting on 22nd and 23rd April 1994." [Interpretation] Then I repeat to him that I'm going to do my utmost to have these done -- these things done urgently so. So in these two paragraphs, it can clearly be seen that my role and my efforts to assist both sides in order to reach an agreement or, rather, to have this focal point of crisis resolved at that moment, resolved, this was a cause of concern to everyone. And it was called Gorazde. Is that right, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've drawn attention to paragraph 19 of this report on page 10, and you refer to the section: "My Special Representative spoke with President Milosevic." Now, the reason Mr. Akashi spoke with you on that day, which was what, some two weeks, a full two weeks after the meetings on April 22nd/23rd was because of Mr. Akashi's dismay and unhappiness that the full provisions of the -- that agreement had not been satisfactorily implemented by the Bosnian Serbs, and he raised with you several specific points, namely the continuing deployment of heavy weaponry within the 20-kilometre zone --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon for interrupting, Mr. Williams. The point of this, that the Secretary-General says when mentioning me in this paragraph, is this phrase: "who had assisted in the convening of the Belgrade meeting [In English] on the 22nd and the 23rd of April." [Interpretation] That's the only reason why I read this paragraph, because this is connected with the first one, in paragraph 3, where it says that at my invitation they came, both, that is to say, Akashi and de Lapresle, and with you and Karadzic and Mladic and their associates. And then he underlines here that -- he says that I had assisted in the convening of this meeting that led to a solution to Gorazde. When one reads this document, this can be seen clearly. Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I -- you've drawn to my attention and the Court's attention paragraph 19, where you correctly say the Secretary-General says you assisted with that meeting. But the paragraph also implicitly shows that Mr. Akashi was at that point very unhappy with the lack of proper implementation of that agreement by the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were all dissatisfied with the lack of implementation on both sides, but the crisis at Gorazde ended through this agreement; isn't that right or is that not right, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Gorazde by the Bosnian Serb side did cease, but there was never - and I would repeat never - there was never a proper implementation of the agreement that was reached in Belgrade on April 22 and April 23. And in his conversation, and I think also a letter of May 14, which is in this documentation, Mr. Akashi lists the continued presence, for example, of Serb heavy weaponry in the exclusion zone, the fact that a UN convoy had been held up for six days on the way to Gorazde, as well as other violations of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, please look at paragraph 6 of this same report of the Secretary-General. And it says: [In English] "...violations of the cease-fire attributable to both parties between the afternoon of 23rd of April and the morning of 25th of April, 1994, the cease-fire has generally been respected since the later date, with only isolated and sporadic small arms fire. "This first contingent included some 100 infantry" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "civilian affairs and civilian police personnel and was led by the UNPROFOR Head of Civil Affairs, Mr. Sergio Vieira de Mello, and the Commander of Sector Sarajevo UNPROFOR Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brigadier General Andre Soubirou. They were subsequently reinforced to a total present strength of 432, all personnel included." [Interpretation] So this agreement, according to this report, was implemented. As for what happened later, that is not something I'm talking about now. The war went on, but since you refer to my role here, is it being denied that my role was to help find a way out of this crisis And doesn't this clearly show that I could not give any kind of orders to the leadership of Republika Srpska and General Mladic? I could just present every conceivable argument in order to have an agreement reached between them and UNPROFOR. Wasn't that the position, Mr. Williams? Wasn't that clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two or three questions here. First -- the first question is: What was the role of the accused? And it is suggested that he was helping to find a way out of the crisis. Would you agree with that, Dr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- the meetings was clearly convened by President Milosevic. It did lead to the agreement. And as the Secretary-General's report in para 6 quite rightly points out, the cease-fire following that agreement generally held. Equally, in para 17 of the Secretary-General's report, he again lists several incidents of harassment of UN convoys by Bosnian Serb forces. But I accept the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assertion that the attack stopped, and I believe that the meeting in Belgrade and the agreement came from that played a huge role in stopping that attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the next question is this - and whether you feel you can answer it or not, Dr. Williams, is a matter for you. It may be more a matter of what inferences one draws. But as it was put to you, you should have the opportunity of answering it - did it not show, this incident, that the accused could not give orders to the leadership of Republika Srpska and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't quite accept that. I think President Milosevic -- President Milosevic's influence at that meeting was very strong, very strong indeed. He was the principal player at that meeting. I recall one specific incident, which I believe I referred to in my testimony yesterday, when President Milosevic scolded Dr. Karadzic for the continuing blockage of a UN convoy on the way to Gorazde that was held up in a village called Rogatica, and then told him, "Look, sort this out now." And Karadzic, as I recall, left the room and made some phone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, this meeting lasted 18 hours, and it consisted of persuading everyone to agree to the terms for a cease-fire. This was, if I can put it that way, a mediation that was extremely difficult in efforts aimed at having a result reached. And that fact shows that there was no possibility of me being in a position to order someone to do anything. That I criticised the stopping of convoys and things like that is not being denied at all. After all, I did this in public as well. I spoke for the media about this. I said that this was something that should be criticised. I insisted that convoys and hostages should be freed. I insisted that the pilots should be freed. I insisted the refugees should be rescued and that humanitarian aid should be provided, and so on and so forth. So do you understand when you look at this entire range of activities that this has nothing to do whatsoever, with - how should I put this? - chain of command or order issuing or whatever? Why do I need to talk to someone for 18 hours if I can simply issue an order to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The length of the meeting is incontestable. I recall it as being 18 hours myself. But I -- that was the pattern, I think, of -- of the meetings that so often surrounded this conflict and war, and the Bosnian Serbs were reluctant to come to an agreement except upon the best possible terms for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. But this agreement was accepted by both, so it is not being contested, is it, that some kind of a solution was found? It certainly was not imposed on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I think the witness has taken this as far as he can. He's described what happened. And it will be a matter for us -- it will be a matter for us to determine what role the accused played in these events and what the extent of his powers were. It may be a very crucial issue, which we will have to determine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well, Mr. May. This is a very lengthy report. If only that report were to be read, one could see what the situation was actually like, what the true situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, there is yet another report sent from Akashi to Annan, the 13th of April, 1994. Mr. Groome also produced it here. I'm just going to read item 6 -- or rather, paragraph 6 of this report of his, this note that he sent to Annan. [In English] " President Milosevic encouraged me to normalise our relationship with the Bosnian Serbs as soon as possible." [Interpretation] And so on. And then it goes on to say: [In English] "The tenor of the communique of President Milosevic's office on our meeting broadcast on the radio was positive... the serious negotiations leading to global and durable cease-fire." [Interpretation] Is it quite visible here that every effort is being made for an agreement between the UN and the political and military leadership of Republika Srpska to normalise their relations, which would enable further agreements and then to move on towards the main goal, that being the war to end, which was something that was repeated umpteen times. I have quoted quite correctly, Mr. Williams, rest assured. So I am talking about the preparations, the run-up, the efforts being made on both sides for rapprochement views to be achieved so that the problem could be overcome. Is that right, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would confirm your account of the 13th of April meeting that you had with Mr. Akashi in -- in Belgrade. I'm not sure what the question is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The reference is to tab 4, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying -- it says: "President Milosevic encouraged me to normalise our relationship with the Bosnian Serbs as soon as possible." And then he says there was a communique of my office -- "The tenor of the communique of President Milosevic's office on our meeting broadcast on the radio was positive; the emphasis was on the need to cool down and to engage in serious negotiations leading to global and durable cease-fire." So this was a generalised effort and Akashi came to talk to me, to consult with me, and to seek assistance from someone whom he believed could act as an intermediary, and that is how this mediation took place, in fact. Is that right, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you also have here a kind of note from a meeting. This was held on the 23rd of April, 1994, a meeting in Belgrade with Bosnian Serb civilian and military authorities. The very heading shows that it is a meeting held in Belgrade with the civilian and military authorities of the Bosnian Serbs. So it was a meeting between you, and Michael Rose also reports about that meeting between you. I chaired it. "The meeting was chaired by Mr. Milosevic and it was attended by --" and it lists all the people present; Akashi, De Lapresle, and Sergio de Mello. And you quite correctly quoted that I had proposed that a normalisation of relations be discussed between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serbs, that a solution to the Bosnian crisis -- to the Gorazde crisis, and once that crisis has been settled, that the elements for an agreement be discussed for an overall, a general cessation of hostilities. Is that right, Mr. Williams? That is what is noted here.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point 6. Since I have to save time, I can't read out everything, though it would be very useful for us to analyse this document. Item 6: Mr. Akashi speaks about his dissatisfaction in connection with the approaches. And then it goes on to sentence 3 in point 6. "Notwithstanding this complication, he was happy to note -- [in English] "that there appeared to be a general agreement on the desirability of sending troops to Gorazde and suggested that UNPROFOR's original proposal to dispatch one battalion to Gorazde be revived." [Interpretation] And then -- it is not so important. What he goes on to say is not so important later on. The composition of the UNPROFOR battalion, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 16. You should tell us where we are. It's impossible to follow, Mr. Milosevic, with this -- this way you go on. Tab 16, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is tab 16, yes, and paragraph 6, yes. And I don't know which tab it is, but it refers to the meeting in Belgrade. I took out the documents in the order in which they were commented on by Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, what we heard a moment ago from you, in connection with Rogatica, is slightly different. Will you look at paragraph 9, please, Mr. Williams. [In English] "At this point, President Milosevic sought confirmation from the Force Commander" -- [Interpretation] Which means General de Lapresle, right, the force commander? [In English] "The convoy blocked at Rogatica had been 'deblocked.' The Force Commander indicated that he had just been informed that the convoy was still unable to proceed and desired to return to Sarajevo. Mr. Akashi said that if full guarantees could be given that the convoy would not be subject to further problems and full freedom of movement were granted to UNPROFOR and other agencies, he would ensure that another large convoy would be sent to Gorazde the following day. However, the BSA would have to honour a cease-fire agreement in the enclave and this should, ideally, be in place before the convoy was dispatched. In addition, the modalities of deployment of UNPROFOR troops in the enclave must be left to UNPROFOR to decide." [Interpretation] So I am asking Mr. de Lapresle, because it was hovering in the air, this report that the convoy had been blocked. I asked him whether it had been deblocked. He said it hadn't, not yet. And then Akashi says that only full guarantees are provided, then another convoy would be sent the next day. And then Dr. Karadzic gave his assurances that the convoy would not have any further problems. That is in paragraph 10. But he also agreed on the need for a cease-fire. "He insisted that it could only be established with a UN presence in the enclave, [In English] firstly on the BSA side, in whose best interest it was to establish a cease-fire, and then on the Bosnian side. He recommended the details for the deployment force be worked out by UNPROFOR and BSA military representatives." [Interpretation] That is the end. Now, look at paragraph 11: "President Milosevic proposed that the meeting be adjourned."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. You're not going to read out these enormous parts of the statement or whatever, press statement, without asking the witness a question about it. Dr. Williams, you have seen that. Is that an accurate account of what occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is a reasonably accurate account. I would draw the attention of the Court to paragraph 10, which Mr. Milosevic has just read, and Dr. Karadzic's statement, "while he agreed on the need for a cease-fire, it could only be established with a UN presence in the enclave." But of course, it was precisely the Bosnian Serb side which was preventing a UN presence in the enclave and which was holding up this convoy at Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is why I wish to read to you paragraph 11, because it shows, as the whole course of the conversation showed, that it was a difficult and dynamic meeting designed to achieve a solution. And paragraph 11 reads: "President Milosevic proposed that the meeting be adjourned to enable to Force Commander and General Mladic to work out the details of the deployment of an UNPROFOR unit in Gorazde [In English] and that a decision on the same be made 'today (rather than) wait for another meeting while people are dying.'" [Interpretation] You will remember that there were various proposals to postpone the meeting, to think things over, to see how things would develop. And I said, let us have a short break, let the commanders come to an agreement, let us finish this today because people are dying. And that is what it says in your notes. I didn't write it. "He expressed disappointment at any decision to turn back the convoy at Rogatica, stating that such a move would be interpreted as being the result of BSA intransigence while, in actual fact, all obstacles to the convoy's movement had been removed." Didn't they inform us that all the obstacles had been removed? They informed us at that meeting, both you and me, that all the obstacles had been removed. "He strongly recommended that the convoy not return to Sarajevo but remain the night in Rogatica, to be joined the following morning by additional troops. [In English] He further proposed that meeting between de Mello and Mladic focus on agreement on the following: The identification of 3 kilometre zone around Gorazde; withdrawal of heavy weapons from the outer ring of the circle around the town"; [Interpretation] thirdly, "monitoring of the cease-fire and related agreements by UNPROFOR." Then the next paragraph says -- was that how it was, Mr. Williams? Is this a correct reflection of the meeting? Look at the following paragraph, 12: "Following the rejection of the proposals put forward" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal first of all with paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think paragraph 11 is a correct record of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Following the rejection of the proposal put forward by General Mladic in the meeting with General de Lapresle, President Milosevic requested the SRSG" - Akashi - "to put forward UNPROFOR proposals for a resolution of the Gorazde crisis. These proposals, agreed upon on 22nd April and further refined on 23rd, are attached." [Interpretation] So I insisted that Akashi propose -- make his own proposal, and I insisted that proposal be accepted. Is that clear, at least? That is what it says in this report.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help us with the acronym, please, Dr. Williams. SRSG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. It's Special Representative of the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: SRSG is the abbreviation for Mr. Akashi, that is, the person representing the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Special Representative of the Secretary-General. Anyway, Mr. Williams, this is your own press statement made on the 23rd of April, and you announced that the special representative, Mr. Akashi, and General Bertrand de Lapresle had talks in Belgrade with the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, including Karadzic and the commander of the army, Ratko Mladic. And you say at the end of the paragraph: "The talks, hosted by the Serbian President, Mr. Milosevic [In English] were aimed at securing an immediate cease-fire in Gorazde and the urgent deployment of UNPROFOR troops in the town." [Interpretation] You're practically confirming what actually was agreed there. You referred to the Nordic battalion, what they accepted, that is, the representatives of Republika Srpska. And I believe that is not in dispute. This is your own press release confirming all this. Is that right, Mr. Williams -- press statement, rather?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I can't find the statement immediately to hand now, but you're -- I think you're doing a very correct reading of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can let you have a copy, if you'd like to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... of the document, front page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then again you have a report to Annan, sent by General de Lapresle on the 25th of April, 1994, which actually confirms the success of the agreement reached. In paragraph 1 it says: "The situation in Gorazde has stabilised as the BSA forces have completed their withdrawal to the 3-kilometre line agreed upon between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Akashi in Belgrade. This phase of the operation is now complete."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I don't have time now to cover all these documents, but I would like nevertheless to draw your attention to the fact that even when Mr. Akashi complains to me, and he sends me a letter -- a copy of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. letter that he sent to Karadzic, he says, addressing me: "As you may know, the situation around Gorazde continues to be difficult. The implementation of the agreement reached in Belgrade under your outstanding leadership has encountered some insuperable difficulties. I have taken the liberty of enclosing a letter sent to Karadzic," et cetera. I am emphasising here the fact that Mr. Karadzic is paying tribute to the efforts invested to achieve the agreement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Akashi; interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this was a turning point, I would say, for the events in Bosnia. Now, Mr. Williams, I have here with me -- we have now established that when there were obstacles you informed Akashi, then Akashi writes to Karadzic, Karadzic responds that this was caused by local inhabitants in uniform but that no one was shooting. I won't delve into that. The problem provoked by the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska are immediately reported to the top - that is, Mr. Akashi - even when there are no casualties, but simply men in uniform. Now, look at this UNPROFOR report, Sector Sarajevo, sector commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if the witness agrees with what you're putting. We are in fact in tab 18, for the record. Dr. Williams, do you agree with what the accused is putting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, no, I don't, Your Honour. In fact, it's not just a question of men in uniform. If you look at Mr. Akashi's letter of 10 May, he lists a series of very serious violations of a cease-fire by the Bosnian Serb forces, including the presence of heavy artillery and convoys being held up for six days, and so on. So it's not a light matter of simply some uniformed soldiers being in places they shouldn't be; these are serious violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I have it here. I picked up the letter again, though I had put it aside. Yes, they are serious violations, and I agree with Mr. Akashi, but the violations regard mostly militiamen, as he puts it, "but also, as late as Sunday, 8 May, infantrymen - remain present..." So it says that they remain present within a radius of 3 kilometres around Gorazde. So this is paragraph a). There's no fighting. There's no combat. There's no shooting. It just says that they remain present. I agree that it is serious, but there's no conflict there. And then b), it says: "On 8 May, two 20-millimetre anti-aircraft gun systems --" and the registration numbers are given -- "were found within the 20-kilometre exclusion zone." So when they carried out inspections, they found another two guns, they registered their numbers. They were under a tarpaulin. They were covered. And they were towed from Rogatica towards Gorazde. Now, there -- where they were being taken, it doesn't matter; they shouldn't be there. And he says it's a violation of paragraph 2 "of our Belgrade agreement." And he's writing this in his letter to Karadzic. Et cetera, et cetera. So the letter refers to certain details regarding the presence of troops and weapons that had still not been withdrawn. But this is certainly important, and I am not objecting in any way to what Mr. Akashi did. But please look at this report sent by Colonel -- chief of staff, Colonel Sonnic. This is 00552739 ERN number. I received this under Rule 68. I think it was not in any of the tabs. It may have been, but I'm not sure. And it's addressed to General Karavelic, the 1st Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it says: [In English] "Sir, on March 27, at about 4.00 a.m., the Bosnian patrol launched a deliberate attack at two Serb observation posts deployed at grid 80378 --" [Interpretation] these are the elevation points. [In English] "Three soldiers were killed and five wounded on the BSA side. The Bosnian side had one man killed. Our investigation has shown that this attack was deliberate and prepared in advance. I strongly protest for this aggressive act against the Serbian side and consider it as a direct violation of the cease-fire agreement provocative as to both Serbian side and UNPROFOR." [Interpretation] Mr. Williams, as I have already said, I have no remarks to make regarding Mr. Akashi's complaints regarding the noted presence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we're not going on like this. I don't know how long you've been speaking for. Let the witness -- if you want the document exhibited, let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, have a look at that. Have a look at that and see if you agree that it's as the accused has put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was just reading from the document.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- it's not a very clear document, I'm afraid. I mean, it -- it gives a grid reference, which -- you know, unless I have a map before me, I -- but as far as I can see, this doesn't refer to Gorazde, Mr. Milosevic. This refers to an incident in Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what is the -- just a moment. Can we have a date, please, Dr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a date on the document. It's dated the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So it's about this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's before any of these talks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no indication of where the violation occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The inference must be that this is in Sector Sarajevo. Now, clearly, it is a serious incident, as Mr. Milosevic points out. It is an attack initiated by Bosnian government forces. Three Serb soldiers are killed, one Bosnian, and so on. I don't contest that at all. I'm sure this is an accurate reflection of a serious incident. But it is in no way comparable to the assault which was taking place at that time on the UN safe area of Gorazde. I mean, this talks about four deaths. How many people do you think were killed in Gorazde? I mean, this is one single incident in Sector Sarajevo, which I don't deny for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will exhibit that document. We will give it the second -- the first exhibit, Defence exhibit, will be the UNPROFOR document referred to earlier, of the 11th of May, referring to the Washington Post article inquiry. That will get the first number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Defence Exhibit 148, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the recently exhibited document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Defence Exhibit 149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's half past 10.00. We're going to adjourn now. The accused has another 25 or so minutes left. Dr. Williams, would you have a word with Mr. Groome just so you can explain your position to him. There will need to be some further examination, I anticipate. Have the amici any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I could anticipate 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Groome, would you please have a word with the witness. And we need to work out a timetable. We have the note about his attending a meeting. Perhaps you could see with him whether it's possible of him to stay or whether he must go, in which case whether we could finish or not in time, what time he needs to go --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- or whether he could stay in fact. Dr. Williams, I'm -- if you have an important matter to deal with, of course you must -- you must go. And you will have our permission. But it may mean your having to come back. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good. I'll do my very best to see if I can stay today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're told there is a flight that's booked already, but perhaps that can be looked at. Thank you very much. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, you've -- you've resolved the situation, I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have made a reservation on a 3.00 flight for Dr. Williams. I believe I only have five minutes of re-examination. And I believe, from what I recall of what Dr. Williams said about the meeting, it's a rather important meeting. So if it's possible for him to make the 1.00 flight, I think that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what time does he have to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They tell me he'd have to leave at quarter to 12.00 but I think perhaps even 12.00 we may be able to get him on the plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm very sorry, Mr. May, that many questions will remain unanswered. But I'll try and put at least a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago I showed you the protest sent by a colonel of UNPROFOR to the Muslim side. However, the point of my question is this: In view of the fact that you personally, by virtue of the office you held, that of a man who provided the whole world with information as to what was going on, did you about those violations and generally about the conduct of the Muslim side inform the world, as you did -- as you informed it about the conduct of the Serb side? Can you say of yourself that you did indeed do that, that you did it in an unbiased way and - how shall I say this - on a footing of equality, that you did it equally for both sides?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I think I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Evenhandedly?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I believe I can say that unequivocally the incident that you referred to, for example, I am sure that my press spokesman in Sarajevo would have spoken to and indeed possibly released that document that you brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I hope you know that General Michael Rose has published a book and the title of the book is: "The Mission in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't suppose you're questioning either his stature or the fact that he, as an honourable man, endeavoured to show the situation objectively.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he says, for example, in that book of his, that is the Serbian translation on page 297 of the book: "The air force offensive of NATO was not a signal only to the Serbs that the peace mission had been rejected and that the West was preparing to apply a higher degree of force than before, it was also directed to winning over internal political forces in America for a resolution to the conflict by war." Now, was that, among other things, the result and consequence of a distorted picture and unobjective information as to what was actually going on? Just give me a yes or no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't possibly give you a yes or no answer to -- to that question. It's very unclear to me what the question is, to begin with. I'm afraid I must ask for it to be formulated in a way that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's start with this: We've got the quotation from the book. Do you think you can comment on the quotation as it is -- as it is on the screen or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the book, as Your Honour will know, is a memoir written some years after the conflict. I mean, it is true that the West, by which one means NATO, became more engaged from 1994 onwards. I would remind the Court that it was a NATO ultimatum in February 1994 which brought about a cease-fire in Sarajevo. And important though the talks were that were held in Belgrade in April 1994, it was also the case that there was again a NATO ultimatum. Without it, frankly, I don't believe the Bosnian Serb forces would ever have agreed to a cease-fire. So in that respect, there is some truth in what General Rose says in that observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of your profession or the office you held at that point in time, and with respect to information, that's what I'm referring to. I'm going to quote from page 333 of the Serbian translation, where it says: "The UN was not able to convince certain important names that too much propaganda would only make the situation on the ground worse. The permanent and uncontrolled publishing of images and pictures of war devastation and unobjective criticism made the situation in Gorazde, Bihac, and Sarajevo more exaggerated, which was designed to up the level of force." Is that what happened? Do you agree with General Rose and his observations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, no, I don't agree with that comment at all. In fact, I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. No is answer. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must be allowed to answer, you having put that to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have always regarded it as absolutely imperative that where conflicts and wars take place it is of great importance that those conflicts are brought to the wider attention of the international community, and I believe the media and the press have a very important role to play in that regard. So no, I don't agree with that statement whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you agree with this, something else he says, on page 304: He says: "I was particularly angry with the journalists because of their biasness, lack of objectivity, and the way in which they reported on the events in Bosnia. Most of the comments from journalists from the east coast of the USA during the Gorazde fighting in 1994 did not write about the suffering and difficult economic situations suffered by the population but of the devastated and looted houses. The truth was different, however. Those houses, which they took pictures of, that is to say, the US reconnoitring airplanes during the air attacks on Serbia, were destroyed and devastated mostly in 1992, when the Serbs and the Muslims were struggling for supremacy in town and when the Muslims thwarted back and refuted the Serbs. They were Serb houses, in fact, left without roofs, without window frames and doors, which the Muslims had looted completely and left empty. It was more than obvious that they had not been destroyed that particular year either during the fighting that took place in Gorazde." Now, my question to you is this: Is it possible that during the time of your mission you did not know about that, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Know about what? That there was destruction on the Serb side as well? Of course I was aware of that. I find it difficult to make a comment on the passage you've again quoted from General Rose. I don't think I have anything further to add on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he says that he was particularly angry with the journalists because of their bias and unobjective reporting, taking one side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In your view, Dr. Williams, when you were in Bosnia undertaking the work, did you find the journalists' reporting on the whole to be biased and one-sided, or can you not say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can pass a judgement on that, Your Honour, and I think I'm qualified to do so. The press corps was very large, very varied. I found on the whole that its assessments were objective. There Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were quite a number of journalists whose reporting of the war was absolutely outstanding. Yesterday, for example, we saw a document from the Reuters correspondent Kurt Schork, a distinguished war correspondent who tragically lost his life in the Sierra Leone conflict two or three years ago. General Rose had a difficulty with journalists. He didn't get on very easily with them. The quotation reveals a very subjective assessment, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is a subjective assessment on the part of General Rose, and you don't agree with it. Fine. Now, do you agree with this, something else he says: "During the previous three years of a bloody civil war, all the protected areas, including Sarajevo, survived and the Serbs did not win control of them, although they could have done, they could have conquered them. Had the Serbs wished to take them over, the state of Bosnia would have ceased to exist. Neither NATO's -- NATO's air force would not have been able to prevent it." Now, do you consider this assessment on the part of the UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be correct or not? And it does go against the grain of what you're saying, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the first part of the statement you read is correct. I think the Bosnian Serb forces quite possibly could have overrun most of the declared safe areas. Certainly I've referred earlier in my testimony to the disproportional -- disproportionality between the two sides to the conflict, the fact that the Bosnian Serbs had so much heavy weaponry. With regard to the second part of General Rose's statement, I don't agree at all. NATO forces, I believe, could have intervened forcefully at any juncture and could have stopped that assault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just indicated and pointed to the differences between what you say and what the UNPROFOR commander of the day, Sir Michael Rose, says. Now, as you said that supplies were made impossible, that it was impossible to bring in supplies, and this because of the conduct of the Serb side, he says on that same page: "Nonetheless, the Serbs never stopped convoys from coming in in order to merit a response from UNPROFOR on a military level, even at the time when the Serbs were said to stifle Sarajevo and strangle it, and the warehouses -- food warehouses in town were not completely depleted. Gas and water was brought in in smaller quantities, as was electricity. There was sufficient quantities of electricity as well." Would that be correct or not, or is General Rose speaking untruths?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me again, taking a passage out of context, not knowing what he's -- the time period he's referring to. But there was sufficient documentation yesterday, and I refer in particular to the -- I'm afraid I can't recall the tab reference now -- the letter from Mr. Eagleton, the senior UN civilian official in Sarajevo, of September the 15th, where he complains about the fact that all gas supplies to the city have been closed by the Bosnian Serbs. On a sort of anecdotal and subjective level, I can tell the Court that on many visits to Sarajevo it was abundantly clear there was no water, electricity, or gas. I mean, that was simply a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit Dr. Williams has referred to is tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, you said you don't know -- didn't know to which period that referred to. I quoted General Rose, who says, "Not even in 1994, when the Serbs were accused of strangling Sarajevo, the warehouses in town had not been depleted." So it refers to this critical year of 1994. And do you agree with the following assertion, which says: "In 1994, according to American sources, the number of persons killed, mostly soldiers, did not exceed 3.000, which was far below the widespread rumours that were going around as to a large-scale genocide which was rampant in the country, which many propaganda people tend to stress"? Now, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you -- "in 1994 the number of persons killed" - wait a moment - "mostly soldiers did not exceed 3.000." What area does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole, and this is from Michael Rose's comments at the end of his book, on page 309 in the epilogue where he says, "According to US sources, the number of soldiers killed did not exceed 3.000, which was far below the widespread rumours that were being propagated about a large-scale genocide." So that's what I'm talking about. I'm saying what he claims for 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to comment on that figure. I would point out that General Rose's statement refers only to the number of soldiers killed. It does not say anything about the number of civilians killed in 1994, which I think is -- is difficult to make an assessment of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. What he says is that a total of 3.000, mostly soldiers - 3.000 and mostly soldiers. So that refers to civilians as well, Mr. Williams. I hope that's clear to you, and it's evident from the quotation. Now, as you yourself dealt with information and propaganda - and I'm going to finish quoting from General Rose's book with this next question - he describes the visit by General John Galvin, the special advisor to President Clinton who arrived in Sarajevo, and I'm going to read out this passage, it's page 107 of his book. And I'm going to read out in detail. "It was early morning," he says, "when we found ourselves near Tuzla. Our escort, a lady from the American Embassy, suddenly pointed to the villages that had been burnt down and houses burnt down that could be seen on Mount Zvijezda and she said to Galvin in a spiteful voice, 'Take a look at what those Serb criminals have done.' Every time Simeon Shadbolt [phoen] had to explain to Galvin why a mosque had been --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. What is the connection with the witness? This is a visit by an American general to Tuzla. And so far there have been references to people from the American Embassy. There is no connection that I can see to the witness. Now, what -- what is the connection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about propaganda. And what I want to ask Mr. Williams is whether he agrees with what General Rose writes. So this particular event, it's a very brief reference, and I would have concluded it had you not interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
