utterances.text: "He had to explain to Galvin why a mosque had remained standing whereas all the churches had been destroyed, because it was quite obvious that the Muslim forces were responsible for ethnic cleansing in that area of Bosnia. It was clear to Galvin too that this woman from the embassy, an employee of the state department --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. It seems to be pointless. The witness can comment on some of the things which General Rose has said in his book, some of them, which he knows about. He can't possibly comment on this visit. But what you can answer was the point that the accused made at the very beginning. You yourself dealt with information propaganda. Is that a fair characterisation of your work, as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't accept that characterisation, Your Honour. I and officials who worked with me strived as best as we could to present an objective assessment to the outside world of the conflict. Mr. Milosevic referred earlier to the international press corps in Sarajevo. You would find, if you look back on newspapers like the Washington Post and the New York Times, for example, that they often criticised the UN because they believed that it strove too far for objectivity and it was accused of bias towards the Muslim side or towards the Bosnian government side on many occasions. We did have difficulties, and frankly one of those biggest difficulties was the absence of information about the Bosnian Serb side, about the Republika Srpska. And that was because of the prohibition by the Bosnian Serb authorities on the UN and on the international press corps working in their -- the areas in which they administered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just quoted examples, but let's not waste time. Mr. Groome provided us here with a document, and you spoke about the -- where non-Serbs were expelled from the Bijeljina region, and the 6th of September, 1994, is the date, sent to Mr. Akashi and Kofi Annan -- from Akashi to Kofi Annan, in fact. And it says if following: "At the time, Dr. Karadzic attributed the problem to the criminals and undertook to replace the chief of police, [In English] due to what he acknowledged was a very unsatisfactory situation in the area with respect to security and crime." [Interpretation] And then he goes on to say -- Akashi goes on to say, "I have subsequently learned that the chief of police has indeed been replaced."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What tab number are we on? Mr. Milosevic, would you in future take a note of the tab numbers, because it's impossible to have a cross-examination without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it's tab 27, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph says, when it says that he learnt that the chief of police really had been replaced. And then at the end he say, "Today I telephoned Dr. Karadzic to ensure that he was aware of the events around Bijeljina and to express our strong concern. [In English] Dr. Karadzic has taken measures to identify, arrest, and prosecute those responsible." [Interpretation] Therefore, does this document show that Mr. -- where Mr. Akashi says that the chief of police had indeed been replaced, that it was such chaos and that it wasn't possible for the leadership of Republika Srpska to keep everything under its control, that measures were taken to protect the population, who were non-Serbs and who were exposed to this kind of pressure, crimes, and so on, or whatever you like to say or call all this, and that as you can see from this, Karadzic did intervene in order to protect them? Is that clear and obvious or not, Mr. Williams? From the document, from the document sent by Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe it's clear. Mr. Akashi hoped that Dr. Karadzic might be taking some measures. But I would refer the Court to another document in this same tab, a letter of the 20th of September, two weeks later, when Mr. Akashi writes again to Dr. Karadzic and says that the expulsions are continuing, that there have been 700 on one single day alone, the date of 17th of September; and Mr. Akashi felt the circumstances were now so serious that he for the first time drew Dr. Karadzic's attention to the possibility that these actions might be the subject of investigation by this very court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All I wanted was to have your comments on the document, and you can see that Karadzic ascribes this to criminals because he didn't replace the chief of police and takes energetic measures to take into custody and send people to trial who were the perpetrators of acts of this kind. Isn't that what this document by Mr. Akashi says?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Akashi hoped that Dr. Karadzic would take measures. It is clear that a single police officer could not have been responsible for the expulsion of 5.000 persons during the period we are talking about, September 1994. Moreover, perhaps a police officer was removed or not. What is clear is that no charges or misconduct or anything were ever pressed against any officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this must be your last question. You've gone beyond your time. But you can ask one more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really don't know what to say. I was going to comment the meeting in Karadjordjevo with Akashi, for which he says we discussed in an informal setting three main items, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, if I don't have the possibility of going into that, then, Mr. Williams, I have a letter by Mr. Akashi sent to me on the 29th of December, 1994, and I'm just going to ask you something with respect to the first paragraph. It says: [In English] "Dear Mr. President, I've come to the end of my first year as a Special Representative of the Secretary-General for the former Yugoslavia. I would like to express my warmest appreciation to you for your fine cooperation and your continued efforts to resolve the terrible crisis in this beautiful land." [Interpretation] I don't want to read any further, but this is a letter by Mr. Akashi sent to me. You can take a look at it if you like, Mr. May, or not, as you wish. Now, Mr. Williams, does this confirm and completely coincide with the context of the explanations given of the activities which, for example, led to a solution to the problem of Gorazde or to solving the other problems that existed? And I had in mind the question linked to Krajina and other parts where what was the activity of Serbia and my own personal actions and as they related to achieving peace first and foremost. And I've read out just the first sentence of that passage.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the letter now. Yes. I remind you and the Court that the agreement reached in Belgrade in April 1994 had six points, only one of which the -- namely, the cease-fire was -- was implemented. I mean, Mr. Akashi's letter is a letter of greetings for the -- for the new year, and I think, you know, it has to be seen in the context of diplomacy and of his wish that this terrible conflict could be brought to an early end, and clearly he saw you as playing a key role in that. I think that is undeniable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give that the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May by allowed to ask one more question, please, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can. But we'll give this an exhibit number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 150, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're a professional, Mr. Williams, and you said during the examination-in-chief that the Serbs did not make any difference, did not differentiate or did not succeed in doing so - I don't know whether I've noted it correctly - between civilian and military targets. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said words to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then, please. When you bear in mind the experiences gained with the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia, when on several occasions it was civilian targets that were targeted, did NATO distinguish or make a difference between civilian and military targets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for the witness. That's just a comment we'll have to consider in due course. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, first of all, just an overview from the last-but-one question that you were asked concerning the influence of Mr. Milosevic. The picture you have given is of the parties on occasion - and by that I mean the Bosnian Serb leadership - assembling in Belgrade periodically before Mr. Milosevic as president of the Republic of Serbia as a bid for him to use his best endeavours to exert political pressure on the Bosnian Serb leadership. Is that right as a picture?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is. One thing I would point out: I think during the period when I was an official in the former Yugoslavia, I think the -- the meetings that we've been talking about in April 1994, I think that was probably the only occasion when the entire Bosnian Serb leadership were brought together with President Milosevic and the UN. I mean, normally these meetings were handled on a bilateral level in Pale or, on one occasion, in Geneva. But I think the gist of what you've said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not surprising in a way, as Serbia was a political power in the region with which you were dealing.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just moving on from that, as we've seen through the obviously limited documents that you've produced, that there was a great deal, and in fact the majority of it, was bilateral negotiations direct with -- with Pale. And by that we mean Dr. Karadzic and/or General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And your assessment of General Mladic was that he had firm control over his forces and was in possession of a disciplined military structure.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Over which he exercised control in a firm and decisive manner.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in the documents that you have produced, either statements or references and notes that you have made during your period of involvement, you were able to see on many occasions intemperate, otherwise called hot-headed, responses by him to situations of the slightest provocation by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's a quote somewhere by you that he couldn't believe that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Muslims would have the temerity to fire on Serb forces and was going to provide a damaging response to any such provocation.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your dealings with the other side, no doubt you were aware as well that any provocation, however slight, was able to engender such a disproportionate response by him.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was a feature of the conflict that was understood and it was a feature that could be used for political advantage by the other side; and by that, I mean the other side to the General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is also a record by you of the meeting in Belgrade at which he was present, at which the threat of NATO airstrikes was being used against the Bosnian Serbs, and he spontaneously uttered, "You'd better hold to your word. If there is NATO bombing, we will attack Muslims and you."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was on the Saturday morning of the 23rd of April. I recall it very vividly. It was about 11.00 in the morning, towards the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The majority of your dealings being with the Bosnian Serbs, you were turning to President Milosevic in situations such as those for him to try and bring his influence to bear upon at least that party to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a correct assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was a situation that you recognised he could bring influence but not control.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could certainly bring influence to bear. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But not control. What was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina was under the control of Karadzic and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the political leadership -- sorry, Dr. Karadzic was the -- the chief political leader of the Bosnian Serbs; that is correct. General Mladic was the commander of the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army, which had, I believe, very close ties to the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can look a little bit at one or two matters very, very briefly. Tab 34, paragraph 11, the meeting by Mr. de Mello on the 11th of August, 1994, with President Milosevic. This is the meeting in which the statement was made about Brazil and the borders as it was part of the process to try and secure the borders because of the imposition of sanctions. Those sanctions were being viewed, certainly from your position, as something that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was taking seriously against the Bosnian Serbian leadership.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, they were a welcome measure. They'd been imposed by Mr. Milosevic, if I recall, on the 4th of August. So it was early days at this stage, 11th of August, to make any assessment of how effective they were, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A device whereby he was trying to influence the Bosnian Serb leadership to take a more constructive role in the peace process.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an -- in particular, it was to try and bring them to agree to the contact group peace plan for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was part of a series of engagements to try and restrain them and bring them into line with his way of thinking in relation to the peace process.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just looking at paragraph 11 of this document, where President Milosevic assured that he had exerted and would continue to exercise his influence in support of the negotiating process.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what he said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And he also said, in conclusion, in paragraph 13, "We have made the choice for peace."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's his statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's for others to judge whether that is right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But that is the context of those remarks.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to go back a bit to tab 4, a slightly earlier stage at this stage, the 13th of April, 1994, the meeting with President Milosevic in Belgrade. And it was in paragraph 2 that the Prosecution directed your attention to a statement by President Milosevic concerning the Serb attack on Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the remarks made by him. I think you will agree with this, that he was not on the ground, so to speak, in Gorazde at that time in April of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I would expect President Milosevic to have been very, very well informed of events. I remind the Court that Gorazde is about 30 minutes' drive from the Serbian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's "information," which is the key word and the next question I was going to ask you about. Information for his purposes could just as much come from Radovan Karadzic and General Mladic as anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And any statement made by him may not be his own assessment in the sense of what he has seen and heard but may be on the basis of information that was given to him.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you're going through these political negotiations and processes that you have described, that is often something that you are up against.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ensuring that the party you're negotiating with has a brief, so to speak, that comes from a disinterested perspective as you would see yourself.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But what was ever -- whatever was said in paragraph 2 thereafter, there is no doubt that President Milosevic was emphasising the need for peace and for a solution of the conflict. We can see in paragraph 4: "President Milosevic stressed that in his view the only reasonable approach towards peace is to seek the general cessation of hostilities."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was his view. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was a series of manoeuvres that took place thereafter involving your parties, so to speak, and him and others in a bid to get the peace process on the road.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A number of initiatives were taken up. We've no need to go into that detail. We don't have time. But this was a part of that process.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see at paragraph 6, at this stage he was of the view, and no doubt you were of the view, that there was a strained relationship between the international community and the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so. Very much so. And they were holding up our convoys, preventing our deployment in Gorazde. The relationship was very strained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the bid was afoot thereafter to try and normalise that as much as possible, to try and get them on side in relation to what they -- their acts and conduct.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move from this document, which is of the 13th of April, and go to tab 16, which is the 23rd of April. I just want to look at the first page, because it's a -- a point there, 23rd of April, 1994. This is the page that comes after your press statement, from Mr. Akashi to Kofi Annan. We see it seems to be typed in "as well as with President Milosevic" in paragraph 1, concerning the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whoever was typing this was -- was presenting it really as a copy of the record of their meeting in Belgrade with Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic initially, and then as an afterthought, well, President Milosevic was there. But again, he was being used as a means of -- of influence, if possible, upon these two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The meeting opens up with President Milosevic presenting a proposed agenda focussing on the normalisation of relations between UNPROFOR, the issue we've just referred to, the solution to the Gorazde crisis, and the cessation of hostilities. It's Dr. Karadzic thereafter who invents or produces a number of reasons in contradiction to those proposals by President Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- if we read the content of this. We don't have a great deal of time, I make that as a general point, but it's quite clear that all sorts of reasons come out presented by him as to why it can't work, what he wants, and what his demands are.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd accept that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And eventually, after that meeting - if we go to tab 17 - that date of the 25th of April, 1994, we see here the code cable which is part thereafter of the initiation of a cease-fire arrangement around Gorazde and an attempt to normalise relations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The breaches that occur thereafter -- and we look at tab 18. After a few days there were breaches and the situation deteriorated. And I won't say it was back to place 1, but it was well on the way of -- of going backwards again. Those points and objections were being made to Dr. Karadzic as for what was going on and happening in relation to those failures.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've principally dealt with the Bosnian Serbs. Concurrently there was also the issue concerning Martic and Babic in the Krajina. And I have a letter here that was sent to President Milosevic by Mr. Akashi, dated the 7th of December, 1994. And perhaps you could take a brief look at it, as it will be the last point I make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One for Their Honours, the Prosecution, and the Registry. It's a document from the Rule 68 material, Your Honour, dated the 7th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you just identify it as being Mr. Akashi's signature and his letter; you may even remember it.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do remember this. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've marked the first two paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- because that's all we're going to deal with, so that our attention is drawn to them. Again, really a replicated role of President Milosevic being asked to use his influence upon Martic, whereas -- is that right? If you could just -- you were nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes. I think that Mr. Akashi believed that Mr. Milosevic could exercise quite considerable influence over Mr. Martic. You will recall in my testimony yesterday I think we referred to elections in the Krajina Serb Republic in January 1994, where clearly Mr. Martic was seen as Mr. Milosevic's preferred candidate in those elections. So our assessment was that Mr. Milosevic could exercise considerable influence with Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But this has to be put into the context of a political power struggle between Babic, Dr. Babic, and Mr. Martic, and Dr. Babic in fact wresting the political initiative away from Mr. Martic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he didn't wrest the initiative completely away but he controlled the local parliamentary assembly and was a powerful figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he was regarded as the more extreme of the two.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he was regarded as being out of President Milosevic's control.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a fair assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at that time, he had more influence than Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Martic was actually formerly president of the Serb Republic in Croatia and the Krajina. I mean, there is a matter of sort of debate as to their relative degrees of influence, but I agree with most of what you're arguing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He'd been undermined by Babic politically, Babic having proved himself an adept and cunning political operator.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome, given the constraints of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll be brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, there's been some discussion about this general cessation of hostilities that Mr. Milosevic was advocating in 1994. This was, of course, after the major ethnic -- ethnic cleansing campaigns of 1992. My question to you is: Had there been a general cessation of hostilities -- had that been adopted at this stage and the current confrontation lines been frozen as territorial boundaries, would one side or another have gained a significant advantage in having that happen?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think yes. I think the Bosnian Serb authorities would have gained a very distinct advantage if a cease-fire was based on the lines of confrontation. I mean, as the Court will be aware, three of the enclaves were completely surrounded by the Bosnian Serb forces - Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica - and Sarajevo itself was besieged. So a cease-fire on those lines would have been self-evidently disadvantageous to the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The accused in his questions to you has characterised his role in the negotiations surrounding Gorazde as simply that of an intermediary between the Bosnian Serb leadership and the UN mission -- a disinterested peacemaker, as it were. I want to draw your attention once again to tab 4 of Prosecution Exhibit 470. The portion I'm going to ask you to look at is being displayed on the television monitors in the courtroom and is paragraph 5. I'm going to read you the first sentence of that. And it says: "President Milosevic emphasised that the current economic sanctions on Serbia should be lifted within the context of a cessation of hostilities." My question to you is: Did Mr. Milosevic introduce the connection between the sanctions that were imposed on Serbia and the cessation of hostilities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I think very, very clearly in that meeting on the 13th of April. So in that sense, I mean, clearly he was not a disinterested intermediary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this the only occasion in which he linked the two, the sanctions with cessation of hostilities in -- or peace in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't believe it was the only occasion, but I can't off the top of my head cite directly a date and place for another occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the question is an unfair one because in the documents one can see that I am talking about the necessity of doing away with sanctions, in view of our constant policy of peace. And that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. It's not an improper question. You can argue the point in due course. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the time that Mr. Milosevic was participating in negotiations - and I'm asking you to consider all negotiations, not simply the ones related to Gorazde - were there still the continuing violations of the closed border between Serbia and Bosnia, a border which as we saw in Prosecution tab 34, Mr. Milosevic had given his personal assurance that it had been hermetically sealed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were documented violations of that border which are clearly documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And my last question to you is: Why was it Mr. Milosevic whose assistance was sought and not the then-president, federal president, Lilic, or the foreign minister, both Serbs and both perhaps more obvious and logical choices, if what was sought was an intermediary or facilitator in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL CHARLES WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it -- whilst Mr. Milosevic may well have been a facilitator, he wasn't an intermediary. It was clearly -- clear that he was a dominant political figure in Serbia and had profound influence on the Bosnian Serb political authorities but also on their military authorities. The other individuals you referred to, Foreign Minister Jovanovic and President Lilic, had -- were thought and I believe assessed correctly not to have any influence on events in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Williams, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we've got this -- we've got the document which was put to the witness by the amici. That can have a exhibit number. Do you want to have it exhibited, insofar as you can?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It better have a C number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Chamber Exhibit Number 7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, a problem arose about this last witness, about his flight, which it may be that he'll miss. I don't have to tell you. It's more satisfactory if we know from the beginning the times, more satisfactory if witnesses are -- it's explained to them that they may have to remain here longer. We cannot guarantee a precise time. It will depend on how long the evidence takes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, all those points will be taken into consideration so far as we can. We do our best to accommodate all interests. We can only forecast for witnesses the approximate time to be allowed in cross-examination, and we are under some constraints, given that there's not a limitless ability to keep people here and to move them backwards and forwards. Indeed, I was going to come to that, if I may, on an associated or nearly associated administrative matter. Next week we are starting with -- we're hoping to deal with several 92 bis witnesses who are essentially only going to be cross-examined. Now, those -- they're here for cross-examination, crime-base witnesses. Those who organise the movements of witnesses and who have to cover the cost of bringing them here and keeping them here are very concerned that we shouldn't have too many with the risk of them having to be sent back. We are, of course, very concerned that we shouldn't have too few, with the prospect of available court time not being fully used. In the Kosovo section of the trial, a pattern developed whereby a particular amount of time was characteristically granted to the accused should he want to cross-examine 92 bis witnesses. Generally he used all the time available to him, although not always. And it was possible to make a reasonable estimate of how many such witnesses we could fit in a particular day. Now, it may be, in light of his greater experience now in cross-examining that he will be able to be more concise in his cross-examining of these witnesses. It may be that other considerations will lead to different times being allowed to him by the Chamber. But we would be assisted if any indication could be given to this, perhaps if not today, tomorrow, as to how much at the most cross-examination time is likely to be afforded per witness in order that we can get the right number of witnesses here but not waste money and resources. Obviously were the accused in any position to indicate that there are witnesses whom he will not wish to cross-examine at all or much, we would be considerably assisted because that will enable us to bring more witnesses in than otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wish to say that this insistence of Mr. Nice's obviously has to do with shortening the time made available to me. This is constant practice here, shortening the time given to me. For example, the witness who's just finished, although you measure the time that Mr. Groome had with him and then you compare it to the time given to me, he presented an entire pile of documents here, and I actually could not even comment upon them or even put a question with regard to these documents. So from the point of view of the principle of fairness as such, my rights are being infringed upon all the time as far as cross-examination is concerned. And if Mr. Nice insists on having these rights curbed even further, this brings us to an absurdity. Does any kind of cross-examination then have any point whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were allowed, with the last witness, longer than the Prosecution, substantially longer. You had every opportunity to put the documents to him. You chose not to take it. You chose, as always, to argue with the witness about some fairly irrelevant matters. Now, of course we have in mind your rights to cross-examine when we consider these matters. It's not -- true, it's not open to the Prosecution to limit your time. All they were referring to in this case was the practice which had occurred with the Kosovo witnesses and asking what our view was about the following 92 bis witnesses next week. We'll consider that. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of other administrative matters before the next witness comes in. Can I just deal with them in private session for a minute?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness and the other gentleman are coming in, can I say the witness list, I think, is coming your way today. I'm very sorry about the delay. I'll explain it to you, if necessary, although I hope that the end of the list itself will be self-explanatory about the task that faces us. And in light of what the accused said very long ago, we of course have absolutely no intention or expectation, let alone desire, of asking for my more time. On the contrary, we very much wish to finish the Prosecution's case as soon as we properly can. But of course time is finite, and you'll see from the witness list that we have a great amount of cutting to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please. Full name, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Peter Woodard Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Mr. Galbraith, you bear the rank of ambassador because, having been educated in Harvard, Oxford, and at Georgetown University, and following a career as advisor to the United States Senate Foreign Relations Committee, you were the United States ambassador to Croatia from June 1993 until January 1998.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Towards the end of your period of work as advisor to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, did you pay visits, or a visit in any event, to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I made four such visits, in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, with a colleague, prepare by August 1992 a report to your committee on ethnic cleansing in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this exhibit has not been formally served on the accused. It's a public document. I'd wish to add it to the material available by way of exhibits for the following reasons: It contains an analysis of what the witness and his colleague found at their visits to the former Yugoslavia in the time given. The document was itself made available to the accused in 1992 and thus constitutes notification to him of the views held of him by others, in this case the authors of the report. So may that document please be produced. It's tab 5 in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was made available to the accused in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The witness will give an account of that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 5. I gather there's a bundle of exhibits. Can they be given a general exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 471.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the witness could have a copy as well. We can look at this document really quite swiftly. If there's a spare copy that the usher could lay on the overhead projector as we're dealing with it, so much the better, but I don't want to take much time with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to the Roman page number V, the letter of transmittal of August the 15th, 1992 and simply the middle of the page, Ambassador Galbraith, as is said there, was this report prepared following your speaking with scores of refugees from, eyewitnesses to, and survivors of atrocities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then pass over two sheets to come to ordinary numbering, pages 2 and 3 at the top. You having already set out some of your key findings as to facts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, make this point on page 2, the first bullet numbered -- or the first bulleted point: "While neither the republic governments of Serbia or Montenegro nor the federal government of the so-called Yugoslavia directly controls the actions of Bosnian Serbs, Serbia and Montenegro share responsibility for the killing now underway in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In May 1992, Serbia withdrew the JNA from Bosnia, but left behind, under the control of the Bosnian Serbs, 85 per cent of its men and most of its equipment." And then you go on to deal further with that in that paragraph. The next bullet point deals with: "Serbian paramilitary groups, including those associated with prominent Serbian political figures, operate with impunity in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And that's all I want from that. Were those your opinions at the time, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On page 3, the centre of the page: "Given the success that," you say, "Serbia has had with its ethnic cleansing policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it may advance the same policy in other areas under Serbian control, namely Kosovo and Vojvodina. There have been signs already that Serbia is contemplating and may have initiated such a course." Well, that may or may not have been prophetic. Can you now identify the particular source or material that led to your then opinion?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This was -- at the time, there was a process of expelling ethnic Croats from the Vojvodina, and some of the other minorities there, and there was acute repression of Albanians in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go over two more sheets on the copies of the document to page 6, we see ten lines down -- eight lines down from the top within that paragraph, this comment: "The Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic has been a proponent of ethnic cleansing but now, with sanctions and the threatened use of military force, would like to disassociate himself from the consequences." It's sometime ago since you wrote the report. Can you in fact identify any particular statement, observation, or anything of the accused that justifies your conclusion or opinion that he was a proponent of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. We believed that Slobodan Milosevic was the architect of a policy of creating Greater Serbia and that little happened without his knowledge and involvement. In this case, we noted that the Bosnian Serb army was created in May of 1992 when the Yugoslav army was dissolved, that it was supported and supplied from Serbia, that Serbia paid the salaries, that the Bosnian Serbs themselves were supplied and supported economically from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But as to any particular observations or statements of his to this effect, anything you can cite or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: No. It was a -- this was really based on, at least as I recall, it was based on behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over to page 8, on the left-hand side, four lines down: "The Serb plan was to connect the Krajina regions of Croatia and Bosnia to Serbia through an ethnically Serb corridor. Refugee interviews permit us to reconstruct what happened in one town in this corridor." The view that this was the plan formed from all the material available to you at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that the Court, and indeed the accused can be reminded of - the Court can have the structure of - your report, your fairly short report, on page 11, under subparagraph -- under paragraph E you make criticisms of the slow international response.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Both of the United Nations and of the United States.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that continues over to the top of page 12, if you wish to read it in detail. There's then a passage starting at page 15 of testimony, which we won't touch at all, but did you speak to these various witnesses yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We spoke to all the witnesses whose testimonies are cited in this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going on to page 26 and then to the right-hand side of that sheet, under "Policy Issues, Serbia's Role," you set out in more detail the passage I've already looked at at the beginning about the governments of Serbia and Montenegro bearing responsibility, and so I needn't repeat that. The second paragraph, you touch on the paramilitary groups, but at the last sentence of that paragraph: "However, there is some evidence that Bosnian Serbs are receiving some financial support directly from Serbia." Can you remember how you sourced that or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. This would have come from information available to the US government. After all, we -- as we noted in the report, we spoke to the embassy in Belgrade and the embassy in Zagreb. It also came from observations made by United Nations officials with whom we spoke, from Croatian government officials with whom we spoke, as well as journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally from this report, under "Sanctions," you set out the reality of sanctions. One thing that may be interesting to observe, in the middle you say that "the most culpable --" the middle of the first paragraph: "... the most culpable party in the conflict has full legal access to international markets and supplies, including oil," observing parenthetically that the Security Council's sanctions resolution explicitly permits goods to transit Serbia, including to Serbian-controlled Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you just explain what was the reality and sometimes perhaps ironic reality of Serbia allowing -- being allowed to be transited by goods that it wasn't allowed itself to receive because of sanctions?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: As you -- Serbia and Montenegro were, of course, subject to sanctions, but the Serb-controlled parts of Bosnia and Croatia were part of the -- legally speaking, part of the sovereign states of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and therefore were not subject to sanctions. And one of the ways in which sanctions were busted in 1992 was that goods would be imported through Serbia, transit Serbia, with a destination in Croatia or Bosnia, but an area under Serbia control, and then re-imported into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's worth observing, finally, as a -- as a place of reference, that on page 35 you list camps and prisons. This report, Ambassador, help us, please, with how it was made available to the accused. I think it was October 1992.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, first the report was released in August of 1992 by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. It received considerable attention in the press. As was the nature of these reports, they would have been picked up by the embassies and, you know, almost certainly copies went to the Yugoslav Embassy in Washington. Then in October of 1992, I travelled to the former Yugoslavia with Michelle Maynard, my co-author of this report, and we went to Belgrade. We had copies of the report with us, and I gave them to relevant officials. I recall giving one to the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Milan Panic, at the time. I did see the defendant at that time, and I may have given him a report, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A convenient moment, then. Ambassador Galbraith, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. We -- I must warn you, as we do all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ambassador, as the ambassador in Zagreb, did you have contact with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Regularly and what sort of frequency?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Extremely frequently. Particularly during the war years I would see him several times a week, sometimes several times a day, depending on the -- what was going on, whether there was crisis, as there usually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Contact with the Serbs in Croatia - Martic, Babic, and so on - what sort of contact with them? What sort of frequency?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Once the -- I became involved in the Croatia peace process, beginning in March of 1994, frequent -- the frequency would average about once a month, maybe a little less, and then in -- beginning in September of 1995, in the -- in the period when we were working the Eastern Slavonia peace process, it was very, very frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From those contacts and from all other available sources, you were able to form a view about the degree to which the accused influenced the Krajina Serbs - this is paragraph 1 of the summary. Can you explain your conclusion as to his influence and over what -- what issues he had influence over?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, first, it was apparent to me that, as indeed it was to virtually all the other international mediators, that the defendant was the -- was the key to any peace settlement, that the Krajina Serb leadership would not take any decision -- any substantive decision for a peace agreement without his approval, that they consulted regularly with him and indeed the leaders with whom I negotiated, at least several of them, Milan Babic, Milan Milanovic, said that they regularly consulted with the defendant. The -- and further, the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina was itself completely dependent on -- on Serbia. The government of Serbia or Yugoslavia paid the salaries of the Krajina Serb military, I believe probably other officials, including the police. This was a completely impoverished region that could not exist even at the very low level that it existed without financial support from Serbia. Supplies came from Serbia. And indeed, when the RSK military suffered a -- a defeat in May of 1995 and when Martic launched rockets on Zagreb, it was -- it was Serbia that changed the head of the RSK army, supplying a new military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to those in detail in just a second. But first, you speak of supplies. Does that include fuel?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How dependent were the Krajina Serbs on Serbia for fuel?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, if you speak of the -- the Western Krajina, or the western part of the RSK, it was completely dependent on Serbia. There was, of course, fuel -- there was, of course, oil produced in -- in Eastern Slavonia, the Serb-held part of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You speak of the change of the head of the RSK army. From whom to whom and how do you assert that it was at the accused's control?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. It was from General Slekotic [phoen] to General Mrksic, and this took place in May of 1995, as I said. It -- it was my judgement that there were a number of reasons. One was the fact that Slekotic had put up no resistance when the Croatians had -- no effective resistance had overrun sector west, and therefore a more effective commander was brought in from the Yugoslav army, and that was where he came from. And also, that -- my belief was that the defendant did not wish to have another rocket attack on Zagreb and he wanted somebody who would not in fact authorise such an attack or not carry out on order to launch such an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps an associated topic is the election of Martic as president of the RSK in 1994. Would you give your account of that election in a couple of sentences and your conclusions derived from it.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was a very peculiar election because in the first round, Milan Babic had about 49 per cent of the vote and Martic had -- his percentage was in the 20s, and yet in the second round Martic had won with 53 per cent and -- to Babic's 47 per cent. That's without precedent in democratic elections. We believed based on sources available to the US government that the election had been rigged to ensure that Martic would win, and Babic himself on the 23rd of January, 1995, told me he believed the election had been rigged by -- and that the defendant had participated in the rigging, that in particular the rigging had taken place with ballots in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn now to the Z-4 process, something of which the Chamber has heard from a couple of witnesses, substantially from the witness Babic. This was a process, "Z" for "Zagreb," and involving the United States, Russia, the European Union, and the United Nations. It lasted from when and until when, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, from March 23rd, 1994, until Operation Storm, August 4th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The overall intended structure of the process?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was a three-stage process that began with the negotiation of a cease-fire in Croatia between the Serbs -- a Serb-held part of the country and the government-held part of the country. That was followed by economic and confidence -- negotiations to award an agreement on economics -- economic and confidence-building measures. And then the third stage was to be a -- a political settlement within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How far did the process get?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: A -- we were able to negotiate a cease-fire agreement on the -- which was achieved in the early hours of the 30th of March. We were, after much, much delay, able to achieve an economic and confidence-building agreement on the 2nd of December, 1994, which however was only partially implemented. And we were unable to present the political plan and to initiate serious negotiations on a political settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll turn to your overall assessment of the participants in a few minutes' time. But at this stage, what was Martic's revealed enthusiasm for the process?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was -- he was, I think, supportive of the -- of a cease-fire, I think extremely reluctant about any kind of economic and confidence-building measures, and opposed to any kind of political settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your judgement, was his approach the result of his own independent judgement or was he guided or driven from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I think he was heavily influenced by the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused's attitude towards the Z-4 process and in particular towards the economic and confidence-building measures, was that revealed to you? If so, when and how?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The accused was actively involved in discussions on the economic and confidence-building measures, not ones - I hasten to add - that I was involved in but that Lord Owen and that Thorvald Stoltenberg was involved in. He offered a -- sought a number of positions, notably trying to avoid any kind of Croatian control of the borders between Serbia and the Eastern Slavonia or between the Krajina and Bosnian Serb territory. That was one of his primary concerns. And in the end, he went along with the conclusion of this agreement, which is why it actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Babic, did you meet Babic at all in 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn of his attitude to or reaction towards the Z-4 process or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did. On -- I first met him on the 23rd of January, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive my interrupting you. Did you learn anything about his reaction in the course of 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, yes. He was a leader in the parliament of the -- of the RSK parliament of the largest political party, and actually he played a -- he was often opposed to the economic and confidence-building measures. I think he saw it as a useful political club against Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You then met him on the 23rd of January of 1995, and that was your first meeting, paragraph 4 I think it is of the perhaps oddly numbered summary. Yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I went down to Knin to brief him on the Z-4 political plan that we were planning to present in the next week. We -- we had lunch, and we had a very engaged discussion. He was intrigued by the plan. He said that there were a number of features of the plan that he thought were very interesting. He said that certainly there was room for improvement. But his -- his general approach was -- was at least interested in it, and seeming that this was something worth pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look briefly at tab 1 of the exhibit. Does this document, Ambassador, set out the draft Z-4 agreement at that stage?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want to go through it in detail. You might, I think, express the view that it was in some ways generous in its terms?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It -- it allowed the Krajina Serbs very, very substantial self-government, indeed almost total self-government in the territory of Croatia, wherein -- where according to the 1991 census Serbs were a majority. So yes, it was extremely generous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For those particular areas.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: For those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we'll just take a couple of examples using the page numbers at the top. On page number 6 we have flags and emblems, it's own flag. Correct.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct. They could have their own flag and their own emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 10 at the top, currency and taxation covered specifically.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. The issue of the currency was a very important one, because they objected to using the Croatia kuna, because they said this was the same currency that had been used by the fascist Croatian state in the Second World War. And so this plan provided that they could have their own bank notes. They would call -- they could call them the dinar or whatever they wanted. They could have their own designs. Although, from a monetary point of view, it would be the equivalent of the kuna and controlled by the Croatian Central Bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see at page 12, its own president, and so on. Yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, thus you're meeting with Babic on the 23rd of January. Had there been a plan that you should meet Martic after meeting Babic?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, there was. If I could just add one other thing to Babic's reaction. In fact, at one stage in that meeting, on the 23rd of January, he was concerned that the plan had actually offered too much autonomy, had been too generous, because he was concerned that it -- it might make the Krajina Serb autonomous entity responsible for pensions and other things, which he had hoped would be picked up by the central government in -- in Zagreb. I said of course that would not be a problem to have less autonomy. We were due to meet Milan Martic in the -- I was due to meet Milan Martic in the afternoon, and Martic cancelled that appointment. He said it was inappropriate for the ambassador -- and a breach of protocol for the ambassador to have met the foreign minister -- the so-called foreign minister before meeting the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll move on in the meetings before we come back to the general character assessment. On the 30th of January, did you and other sponsors of the plan meet with Martic, Babic, and Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about that in a sentence or so.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We -- we had presented the plan as a basis for negotiation, not as a final document -- as a take-it-or-leave-it document to President Tudjman in the morning, and in the afternoon we flew to Knin, where we met in the castle with the top Krajina Serb leadership, including Martic, Babic, and Nikolic. We attempted to hand over the plan, and Martic would not take it. He wouldn't touch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did the meeting end?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, of course we were somewhat shocked that he would actually not even physically receive the plan, much less that he would -- that they would refuse to negotiate on the basis of it. We attempted to persuade them in every possible way that this was not in their interest, that if they refused to negotiate it would increase greatly the likelihood of -- that the Croatians would take military action, that the international community would be -- it would be much harder for the international community to prevent a military outcome. But none of these arguments worked. At the end of the meeting, Nikolic, the so-called Prime Minister, said to us, he said, "You should be -- you should be professional diplomats. You're making a great mistake." And I replied, "A great mistake has been made, but we will see by whom."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think you made an observation that relates to Babic and his approach.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. As we were leaving, Babic came up to me and he said in English, "I'm sorry."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, you'd seen Tudjman in the morning. Was Tudjman ever prevailed upon to accept the proposal?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He agreed to negotiate on it but very reluctantly. However, given that the Serbian side refused even to receive the plan, Croatia's bona fides were simply not put to test.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the accused?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, part of the plan was that we would go to -- from -- we'd Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. present it first to Tudjman, then to the Krajina Serbs, and then we would go to Belgrade. The accused refused to see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 9th of March, did you meet Babic again?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this occasion, the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was to -- we had worked out an agreement in Copenhagen or with Tudjman to extend the United Nations' mandate. It was going to be changed from being an UNPROFOR mandate to being an UNCRO mandate with some essentially cosmetic changes that would keep the UN there. And I went down for the purpose of persuading Babic that they should be cooperative with this, but it also provided an occasion to discussion the Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if anything, did he say about it?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, first he received a copy of the plan, and again he was very interested in different aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come a little later to something else he said about the plan and the reactions to it, but let's move on chronologically to Operation Storm. When did you learn that Croatia was planning military action?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: On or about the 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The apparent reason for this?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was because there -- there was a combined attack from -- by the Krajina Serbs and the Bosnian Serbs on the Bihac enclave. This came shortly after the successful attack on Srebrenica, which had cost 7.000 lives, a successful -- and there was an ongoing attack on the enclave of Zepa. And the -- the Croatians were concerned that if Bihac fell, their strategic position would become much worse because the -- they would not -- the Serb side would not have any internal lines to defend, that is, they wouldn't have to defend against the Bosnian 5th Corps that was in Bihac. They were also -- and that this then could lead to the creation of a western Serb state, a unified western Serb state with the Bosnian Serbs and the Krajina Serbs. Second, they were concerned that they would be the -- that the survivors of Bihac would come to Croatia. And of course they'd already been overwhelmed by several million refugees passing through Croatia during these war years. And finally, they saw little prospect that there would be a peaceful solution to the Krajina problem. They believed that this was an opportune time for them to retake the area because with the events that had happened in Srebrenica, the international community would be disinclined to take any action against the Croatian government for doing something that essentially would save Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the failure of the Z-4 process, which had lasted some eight months or thereabouts and was already a year old overall, did that play a part in all this?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It played a very significant part. The Croatian President Tudjman and his colleagues in the government saw no prospect that there could be a negotiated settlement that would bring about the return of this territory to Croatia or the return of Croatians who had been driven out of the territory. So they felt that the military option was the only one that was available to them. I think that they were contemplating doing it later in the year, in December of 1995, when the UNCRO mandate expired. But what the events in Bihac -- in Srebrenica and the attack on Bihac provided a window of opportunity that they decided to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the accused's attitude to Z-4 process and settlement generally understood, known, and discussed at this time?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was discussed -- it was known at this time. It was continuously discussed by those who were involved in the peace process. I think certainly the Croatian government saw the accused as -- as critical to any settlement. And when they -- when they saw no likelihood that he would agree, this was an important factor in their decision to take military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you on the 25th of July send a cable to the United States Secretary of State giving an account of a survivor from Srebrenica that you'd been provided with?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And although we haven't time for material of this kind, interesting though it is, I think that the material had been provided to you by your wife, is it, or friend at the time, now your wife?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Now my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was an eyewitness account from a survivor.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct; somebody who had been in a group of men who were -- who were -- all the rest -- all but one of the other members of the group were executed. So he was a survivor of a mass execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was the account that you were given and that you were able to draw on for your cable to the United States, was the account detailed as to those involved in the massacre?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And among -- it specifically said that General Mladic had spoken to the group, had told them that they could expect no comfort or help from their Alija, from the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to any unit or troops involved, was the eyewitness detailed on that?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, certainly he described the troops as being -- as Bosnian -- members of the Bosnian Serb army. I don't think in the account that I had that it was -- that he listed specific units, but I haven't gone back and checked the cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you sent that cable to the United States. Did the late-President Tudjman consult you about what the United States' position on military attack would be?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you respond to that? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I responded that -- we delivered several demarches to the Croatian government in this period. The Croatians were concerned that there not be -- that if they took military action, that they would not face sanctions from the UN Security Council for having a wider war. We responded by expressing understanding for the situation in which they found themselves and understanding for the fact that -- that they were prepared to expend blood and treasure to save Bihac. We were deeply concerned that Bihac would fall, that it would become another Srebrenica. It was four times as populous as Srebrenica, so we were concerned that we could see 30 to 40 thousand people being massacred if -- if Mladic and the Bosnian Serbs did the same thing there. We did -- we did not approve any kind of military action, and we pointed out that military action would have serious -- was always a risky proposition, that if Croatia got into any difficulty, it certainly couldn't expect any help from the United States. And I warned Tudjman in the strongest possible terms that should there be any kind of military action, that we would hold him accountable and Croatia accountable for protecting the civilian population, Serb civilians, as well as for making sure that UN peacekeepers in the area were not hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Though you didn't support, did you expressly oppose, or did you leave that neutral?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We neither supported nor opposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Despite what must have seemed -- was to turn out to be an inevitable war, did you make one last effort yourself to avert that consequence?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. Our position on this, the US government position, was as I said - and I just want to emphasise it - very much affected by what was happening in Bihac and by -- we recognised that a war was going to have terrible humanitarian consequences but that the -- that it was a lesser evil than the -- than what we thought was the likely massacre of 40.000 people in Bihac if the Serbs applied Srebrenica rules there. Nonetheless, we wanted to do everything possible to try and find a peaceful settlement, and so when I spoke to President Tudjman on the 1st of August in Brioni, I -- on instructions from the State Department, I raised with him the possibility of meeting Babic in Belgrade later that week. I should preface this by saying the previous weekend I had been in touch with Babic through the United Nations and had proposed a meeting to try and see if we could head off the war. He had said, "You're not welcome to come to Knin, but I'd be prepared to meet you in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who had made you -- who had made you unwelcome in Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But Babic -- and we're going to come to the personality assessments, as I say, later, but Babic was prepared to meet you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Babic said -- right. He said I wouldn't be welcome in Knin, but he wanted to meet me in Belgrade. Tudjman initially said, well, this would be an interesting idea but don't wait until the end of the week; do it right away. And so with -- he, incidentally, a few hours later he had his press secretary call to -- or deputy press secretary call to say maybe it wasn't such a good idea, but the US government was determined to see if there was any hope for peace, so they instructed know go to Belgrade. I went there on the morning of the 2nd, and at 8.00 in the evening, I met with Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 2nd of August, 1995 you met Babic. What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I told him that a catastrophe was about to overtake the Krajina Serbs, that the Croatian government -- Croatian military was poised for military action, that because of the attacks that the Krajina Serb army had participated in into Bihac that there was virtually no sympathy for them in the international community, and that -- that they would have to agree with terms that President Tudjman had outlined to avoid military action. Those terms included a withdrawal from -- of all RSK forces from Bihac, they included reopening a pipeline through Sector North that had been opened by the economic agreement but closed down by the Krajina Serbs, included opening of road and rail links through Knin, and most importantly, an agreement to begin immediate negotiations for political settlement within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly how many items there were in the requirements? Don't mind if you can't.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I think there were seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. What was Babic's general reaction to your proposal?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Babic came alone to this meeting which was held at the American Embassy in Belgrade. His demeanour was extremely serious. He listened attentively to everything I said. And then he replied in the following manner: He said -- he began by apologising by what had happened on the 30th of January. He said that he couldn't -- it was incomprehensible that the Krajina Serb government should have received the representatives of the most powerful countries in the world, that is, the United States, Russia, the European Union, and then to have refused to receive the plan. He had said that this was something that was decided by those higher than him, specifically Martic and Milosevic. He then went on to say that he could -- he could understand fully why the Croatians were attacking at Glamoc and Grahovo, places in the Livno Valley that they had been -- that they'd taken, and why they were poised to attack the Krajina region, that he could not understand the reasons that the -- that his government had launched an attack into Bihac. He said that he would accept the conditions, at least all the conditions but the last one, the political condition, where we had some more discussion. He said that -- he didn't feel that he could say that he would accept a settlement based on reintegration into Croatia. I thought about that. He said, "No political leader could say that." So I said, "Well, as an alternative, why don't you say that you will agree to negotiate on the basis of the Z-4 plan, which is in fact a -- an arrangement to reintegrate the Krajina into Croatia." We had a back and forth about Eastern Slavonia. I said that, you know, it would be impossible to go beyond the provisions of the Z-4 plan on Eastern Slavonia which would not have the special autonomy, because it was not a Serb-majority area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's pause there, because we're taking a lot of information.
