utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I may be allowing you to go just a little too fast. You'd explained earlier that the Z-4 plan was going to provide autonomy for those areas with Serb majority at the relevant census. Eastern Slavonia didn't qualify?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It did not qualify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Other parts did, but not Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Eastern Slavonia and Western Slavonia did not qualify, nor did all of the sectors north and south.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the -- did Babic say anything to you at that stage about why it was that the accused was opposed to this plan? And if not, did you discover from elsewhere why he was opposed to this plan?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: What Babic -- let me, if I can, just explain, I hope very briefly, the -- what came out of the meeting was in fact this agreement, that he would -- he would publicly state his acceptance of all of -- all of these points, but in lieu of saying he would -- he would negotiate on the basis of a reintegration into Croatia he would negotiate on the basis of the Z-4 plan. Further, I told him that the Z-4 plan was unachievable at this point in time, that Tudjman had the upper hand, he would never accept autonomy that extensive, and that the most that the Krajina Serbs could hope for was something that was roughly based on Croatian constitutional law. He understood that. He accepted that. I said, "I will convey this as a private message from you to Tudjman that you understand this, that you're not looking for -- you understand you'll never get the Z-4 plan." He fully agreed. Then came the issue of whether this could be sold to the leadership in Knin, and he said, "Well, my party has a majority in the assembly. I think I can get them to go along." The question was then: Would Martic go along? He said, "One sentence from Milosevic and we can get the agreement of Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he was right about that. Things would not have unfolded in the way they did.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is right. In my view, the war could have been avoided and 180.000 Serbs would not have become refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Babic say anything about efforts he had made at the time to see the accused?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He said that he had tried to see the accused and that the accused would not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the occasion of this -- this very visit to Belgrade or on some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: On the occasion of this visit to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was that account of his consistent with what you learnt of an effort made by the United States charge d'affaires?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. After this agreement was concluded and given what Babic had said about the decisive role of the defendant, and given what we understood to be the decisive role of the defendant, the United States sought to make a demarche to the defendant. The charge tried to see him on the 3rd of August, the next day, to get -- to get him -- to get Milosevic to make a statement of support for this deal, and he would not see the American charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course the charge d'affaires was the principal, the senior diplomat at the time, there being no ambassador in that post.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Babic made his public statement.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did that attract any -- or any significant support?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He -- he made a statement, and the -- there was a meeting in Geneva on the 3rd of August between the Croatian government delegation and a Krajina Serb delegation. The Krajina Serb -- the idea was that the Krajina Serb delegation would be instructed to accept the full package that Babic had accepted. They were certainly ambiguous in their statement. It was not the clear-cut acceptance that was required, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. again I think the reason they didn't make any clear-cut acceptance is that Babic alone -- by this point, incidentally, he was the Prime Minister of the RSK -- didn't have sufficient authority to command the delegation in Geneva. Milosevic, of course, was silent. I flew back to Zagreb, where I saw Tudjman. At the meeting with Tudjman - this was at now 5.45 on the 3rd of August - I urged him to hold off on military action. I said that we would know within a matter of days whether the Krajina Serbs were serious, because there were concrete steps that they had to take, very quickly, and that -- it was important to give -- give a chance to see if they were serious, that -- because the alternative, war, would be so disastrous, particularly for the population of the Krajina region. Tudjman didn't believe that Babic -- that Babic had the clout to deliver the Krajina Serbs, and so he listened, but basically he went ahead with his decision for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look briefly at an existing exhibit, 352, tab 104, a British code cable of August 1995 dealing with these matters. You've seen it before or had the opportunity to see it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope the Chamber has got it before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you reviewed this code cable from your British counterpart?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it accurate, subject to what must be said in paragraph 8?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is accurate. He was a very skilled diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at paragraph 8 he says this: "Commenting on his discussions, Galbraith recognised that Babic might not have authority to conclude a deal on these lines. He might be disowned by his RSK colleagues in Knin and by the Assembly, but it was a last chance for peace. He, Galbraith, would be seeing Tudjman tonight at 5.45 local time to report the outcome of his talks with Babic in Belgrade. Milosevic was being briefed by the American Embassy in Belgrade." Comment?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: At the time, of course I had hoped that our charge would be able to see Milosevic. I expected, given the -- the imminence of war, given that the scale of the military action which was going to be the largest military action in -- in the -- in the conflict since 1992, that of course Milosevic would see the American representative, and I didn't know at the time I briefed my diplomatic colleagues that that was not going to happen. So Ambassador Hewitt accurately conveyed what I said, but of course what I had hoped and frankly expected to happen didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the document ends before the addressees or so on are listed, with a hope that Mr. Roberts can be instructed to take action with Mr. Milosevic. That would be then the British charge d'affaires, Iva Roberts. Did he have easy access to the accused, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I think he had good relations with the authorities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it should have been possible to communicate the state of play to the accused had he been receptive at that time.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It certainly should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Well, following these efforts, the attack began.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The consequences you've already summarised a little earlier. Perhaps this would be a convenient moment for you to give your assessment from all your experience of at least two, possibly three, of the figures you've referred to, in terms of intelligence, ability, leadership, from what you saw. First of all, Martic -- and also influenced by others. Martic?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Martic was a -- a former policeman, I thought a man of very limited intelligence. I didn't think that he had -- although he was the president of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina, I don't think that he had any particular interest in the -- in the people of that territory, and I thought he was way out of his depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Influenced by ...?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: And very much -- well, influenced by the defendant, by the government of Serbia, the Serbian military, the Yugoslav military, certainly would be unwilling to act on a key matter on his own without the approval from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Babic?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Babic was a -- was also a nationalist. And I don't want to convey the idea that there are any saints in this process. He was a nationalist, he was a participant in the creation of the RSK and in the expulsion of the Croatian population. Nonetheless, I thought he was the most charismatic of the -- of the politicians. I thought that he had the interests of the Krajina Serb population much more at heart than any of them. I think he was the only one, actually, who had any concern for the local population. I thought he was easily intimidated, both by Martic and by Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For these two, was cohabitation, living together, a possibility?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, cohabitation with each other was extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Living together, as between the ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: For Martic, it was absolutely out of the question. He said that Serbs -- repeatedly told me that Serbs and Croats could never live together and that if the area was reintegrated into Croatia, that he would not stay. Babic I think was more open to the idea that Serbs and Croats could live together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he popular amongst the people of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was the most popular politician, particularly in the -- in Sectors North and South. He had been the mayor of Knin. And in my judgement, of course, he had -- he was the man who had actually won the election in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if any, control did he have of the army?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He had no control over the army. And of course that's why he was easily -- he was capable of being intimidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving forward. In the course of Operation Storm, did you take a public position on human rights abuses committed by the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I was -- I and the United States government was repeatedly and publicly critical of Croatian human rights violations, which were severe and inexcusable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How regularly, if at all, did you take these matters to Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I saw him on a number of occasions in this period, as well as his chief of staff, Hrvoje Sarinic, and other officials of the Croatian government, and on every one of these occasions I raised the -- our concerns about what was happening to the population in the Krajina, the human rights violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you almost famously on one occasion find yourself on a tractor, preventing violations? And if so, in a summary, tell us how that came about.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. What -- what happened was there was a group of about 40.000 Serb refugees who had -- who had not been able to escape to Bosnia and they'd been surrounded by Croatian forces near Topusko in former Sector North. A cease-fire was negotiated which permitted them to leave -- pass through the town of Sisak and go onto the highway to Eastern Slavonia and possibly then on to Serbia. When the first group of these refugees left and passed through the town of Sisak, they were attacked by a Croatian mob, and it happened that there was an AP - Associated Press - reporter there. And that was late in the evening. I think it was the 9th of August. The next morning, early, I read the story. And it described the attack. It described a mother whose car window had been smashed with a brick, pulling shards of glass out of her baby's blanket. And it described the Croatian policemen standing around, laughing, and basically saying, "These people got what they deserved." I thought that was an outrage. I read the story to Hrvoje Sarinic over the phone, Tudjman's chief of staff. I said if they didn't do anything about it, I would go down and join the convoy myself. I made an appointment to see Tudjman at 12.30. I read him the story. I said that this -- this kind of thing was -- would have a devastating impact on Croatia's relations with the United States, that, you know, he absolutely had to stop it. I said that in a normal democratic country, the Minister of the Interior would have been sacked or resigned in light of this. Tudjman got quite angry, and so I decided that I needed to follow through on my threat to join the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think you went down in an armoured vehicle but --

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I went down in an armoured vehicle to Petrinje, which was -- where, basically, there were no Croatian civilians, it was a military zone. And the convoy was along the highway, and it was stopped, and I -- so I walked along the convoy. My plan was to put my armoured car into the convoy and drive along with the American flag flying, but I ran into a garbage collector from -- who was originally from Karlovac but had moved across the line into the Serbian side. He was quite friendly, recognised me from television, and he invited me to join him on his tractor with his wife and two small children, and so I decided to do that. And I drove with him on the tractor through Sisak. There was a -- a crowd along, jeering, shouting insults, but the Croatian government had policemen every 10 metres and there were no incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other detail from this period. You were, as you've indicated, on television from time to time. You once gave an interview, I think where you made a comment about ethnic cleansing which needs interpretation.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. This was for British television. I think it was the BBC. I said that -- that the -- the Croatians had not engaged in ethnic cleansing in the Krajina, although they had engaged in serious human rights abuses. And my -- my point was that ethnic cleansing was where the forces had come into a town, paramilitaries backed by the military, engaged -- terrorised the population, engaged in killings, rapes, and forced the population to leave. This -- in this case, the population had left before the Croatians arrived, probably rightly fearing what the Croatians might do but nonetheless they were not there when the Croatians actually arrived. And so therefore it wasn't ethnic cleansing. The analogy that I would use is that you might enter a room with intent to commit murder but if the individual whom you intended to kill wasn't in the room and had departed the scene, your bad intent probably isn't a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on to Dayton, your assessment of -- from the things that you had to deal with him over, your assessment of Tudjman as a leader or strategist or tactician at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I thought Tudjman was an effective leader in the sense that he knew where he wanted to take Croatia. He was able -- he surrounded himself with some capable subordinates, such as the Foreign Minister Granic and the Defence Minister Susak. He was able to delegate to them and yet -- and they were able to negotiate on his behalf, and yet he remained in command. To say that he was an effective leader is not to say that his motives were good. He was a nationalist, he had a vision of Croatia that often struck me as being out of the nineteenth century, and he had very little respect for fundamental human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tabs 3, 4, and 5 are slightly out of order. Can we go to tab -- sorry, tabs 2, 3, and 4 are slightly out of order. Can we go to tab 3 first. We've moved on, then, now from August to October 1995. Here is a joint statement issued by yourself and Stoltenberg, reflecting a meeting on that day. Can you tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. Following Operation Storm, the United States took over the peace process with President Clinton's initiative, and a part of that initiative was a settlement in Eastern Slavonia, and I was tasked to handle that part of it. And so I began a basically shuttle diplomacy between Zagreb and Eastern Slavonia. At the end of the month, I joined up with Thorvald Stoltenberg, who was the UN mediator, and so we became a team. We decided that the best way to go after -- we'd had a number of proposals, but by the end of September we decided that what we should do is to get both sides to agree to certain basic principles for a settlement, and we worked the principles with both the Croatian side and the Serbian side, and on October 3rd they held their first joint meeting in Erdut and they agreed to 11 principles that -- well, 10 principles we had prepared in advance and one that was added by Hrvoje Sarinic, the Croatian representative, and accepted by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So tab 3 is the joint statement reflecting what you've just told us; tab 4 sets out the 10 plus one, 11 principles. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again, they're there for reading, we needn't take time on them. The next step, we see from tab 4, was to have been a meeting in Zagreb on the 9th of October. But maybe we can move more swiftly than that. If there's nothing significant there, when's the next significant meeting? Is it the 1st of November?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, there -- there are a series of meetings that continue through October, but this process is not brought to conclusion. And I think at this stage it might be useful for me to explain -- give you my view as to why. The -- at Erdut, both the Croatian government and the local Serb delegation accepted these 11 points. In our presence -- sorry, in their presence, in the presence of the Serbian delegation and the Croatian delegation, Stoltenberg and I held a press conference in which we announced this agreement and everybody -- there was congratulations and so on. That same day, the 3rd of October, Richard Holbrooke, who was engaged in a broader shuttle, was in -- went to Belgrade. In fact, he was almost literally overhead as this was happening, because we spoke briefly on the phone. And he went and saw the defendant. The defendant said that he was surprised by this agreement, he didn't know anything about it, and later he told Holbrooke that no such agreement had been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 1st of November?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The 1st of November, I was in Dayton, and we had -- this was the morning that the Dayton Peace Conference opened. I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were tasked, I think, with dealing with Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: And I was tasked with dealing with Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please, about how that developed on that day.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Holbrooke had decided that Eastern Slavonia should be the first item on the agenda, partly because President Tudjman was there only for the opening of the conference and he was going to go back to Croatia to help form a new government. There had just been elections in Croatia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And also because Holbrooke hoped that if some agreement could be reached on Eastern Slavonia, it might develop some momentum. He had asked me -- I had prepared a -- a statement that -- which basically outlined the basis for normalisation of relations between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and which dealt with the -- said that the issue of Eastern Slavonia should be resolved peacefully and in accordance with the agreed principles at Erdut. Secretary Christopher took this paper. He had bilateral meetings in the morning with both Tudjman and Milosevic. Tudjman agreed the letter -- the statement as I drafted it. Milosevic struck out the provision relating to the Erdut principles. Then in the afternoon, at 5.00, in the Carriage House at Dayton came the first joint meeting between the defendant and President Tudjman, hosted by secretary -- Secretary of State Warren Christopher. President Tudjman arrived promptly at 5.00 p.m. He was joined by Granic, Susak, and Sarinic. On the American side, of course I was there, Holbrooke, and Christopher Hill, among others. President Milosevic showed up about 35 minutes late. The secretary said that he wanted to address the issue of Eastern Slavonia. He asked me to give a briefing on where the negotiations stood. I did. Tudjman listened perhaps somewhat impatiently. He then said, "Look, that's not the key issue here. The key issue is whether Milosevic -- whether President Milosevic is prepared to accept the reintegration of this territory into Croatia." Milosevic said, "Well, there should be a referendum." Now, he didn't actually say what the referendum should be about, simply that there should be a UN administration and a referendum. Tudjman reacted, of course, strongly against that idea. He explained that -- basically said that if this isn't solved peacefully, we'll solve it militarily. Milosevic said to him, "Well, you're a good man, but I can see you're under the influence of your generals." The conversation at this point was getting quite heated. Susak said, "That's completely wrong." There was -- Milosevic turned to Susak and said, "So Gojko, what are you, a general?" And then, just out of the blue, Milosevic said, "Okay. I understand. There won't be any referendum."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there in the narrative, the accused had complete authority to negotiate these matters?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apparently.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yeah, apparently. And indeed he was actively negotiating these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he ever point to there being anybody else who should be dealing with these matters on behalf of the Krajina Serbs or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, he -- he constantly said that this was a matter for the Krajina Serbs, for the Eastern Slavonian Serbs at this point, the local Serbs, to settle. But at the same time, he in fact was the man who was negotiating the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the business of the referendum just raised and dropped like that, did that come with any prewarning at all?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, the referendum had been an issue that had been raised earlier by the local Serbs at the beginning of the negotiation, and I had said to them, "That's impossible." It had been raised by the defendant as late as September 1995 in a meeting with Hrvoje Sarinic in Belgrade, in which he had proposed a referendum, as well as a territorial land swap. So this was a recurrent position from the Serbian side, but it -- it certainly had been dropped by the time the October 3rd principles had been agreed by the local -- certainly by the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The formal part of this meeting, tell us how it ended. And then if we have time, tell us, please, what happened in the 45 minutes that followed.

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, Secretary Christopher left, along with Holbrooke and the other Americans. I stayed. President Tudjman and President Milosevic signed this statement asking Stoltenberg and myself to return to the region, and then Tudjman and his party left and I ended up talking to the defendant for about 45 minutes. It was -- we talked substantively on the issues of Eastern Slavonia. He insisted that Croatia wouldn't dare use military force, that they wouldn't prevail; a judgement I thought was very wrong. He then made -- told me that I wouldn't accomplish anything going back to Eastern Slavonia on this mediation mission, even though he and Tudjman had just signed a statement asking that Stoltenberg and I go back, and that I would do just as well to spend my time on vacation in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You interpreted that observation as revealing what and meaning what?

utterances.speaker: PETER WOODARD GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I interpreted it to mean that a settlement on Eastern Slavonia would not be decided by the local Serbs in this shuttle diplomacy, that -- and certainly not decided by them in Erdut, but it would be decided in Dayton at such time as Milosevic decided it was convenient and useful to him and his broader purposes to settle the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's time to adjourn. Have you very much more?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I think ten minutes tomorrow morning, I should hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Ambassador, would you be back, please, tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: at 1.48 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of June, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
